destinations.risk_summary:
Paris is not dangerous so much as **expensive in ways the booking page does not show, and crowded in ways the opening hours do not warn you about**. Three things account for most ruined Paris trips: a tourist tax that rose sharply in January 2026 and is collected at the property rather than at booking, organised pickpocketing concentrated on a handful of named metro lines, and closures — the Louvre's fixed Tuesday, plus strike days and heat closures that are announced at short notice.

None of it is hard to plan around. All of it is expensive to discover on arrival.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes, and the crowd argument against it is weaker than it sounds — the pressure is concentrated in about six places and four months. The trip that goes wrong here is almost always the one booked on a headline room rate and a assumption that the famous museum is open.

If your dates are fixed and fall in July or August, budget for heat: in late June 2026 the Louvre cut its closing time to 4pm for four consecutive days during a heat wave, and the Eiffel Tower has done the same. That is not a reason to cancel; it is a reason not to buy a non-refundable timed ticket for 5pm in a heat wave.
destinations.worst_months: July–August (heat and peak crowds), and any announced strike day

overview.body:
Paris concentrates an enormous number of visitors into a small, walkable centre served by a dense metro. That combination produces the city's whole risk profile: crowding at a handful of sights, pickpocketing on the specific lines that connect them, and a cost structure with several layers that are not in the advertised price.

The practical read is that Paris punishes assumptions and rewards ten minutes of checking. Check the day of the week against the museum. Check whether your accommodation quoted the tourist tax. Check whether there is a strike on your date.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes. The honest caveat is that Paris in the first week of August is a materially different trip from Paris in early May — hotter, more crowded at the top sights, and with more local businesses closed for the French summer holiday.

If you can move your dates, April to May and late September to October are the window where the weather, the crowds and the prices are all simultaneously reasonable. If you cannot, the trip still works; it just needs earlier bookings and a plan for the middle of the day.

top_risks.body:
- **The tourist tax you were not quoted.** Rates rose sharply on 1 January 2026 and are charged per person per night, collected at the property.
- **Pickpocketing on named lines.** Metro lines 1 and 6, the RER B from Charles de Gaulle, and Châtelet–Les Halles account for a disproportionate share of incidents.
- **The Louvre being closed.** Every Tuesday, all year, plus 25 December, 1 January and 1 May.
- **Strike days.** French industrial action is announced in advance and closes museums and transport; the Louvre itself was shut by staff strikes in December 2025.
- **Heat.** In June 2026 the Louvre closed early on four consecutive days during a heat wave.
- **Timed tickets bought from a lookalike site** at a markup, or that turn out not to exist.

scams.body:
The Paris repertoire is old, well documented and almost entirely based on distraction rather than force.

- **The petition/clipboard approach.** Someone asks you to sign a petition; while you read it, a second person works your bag or pocket. Common around the Eiffel Tower, Sacré-Cœur and the Louvre forecourt.
- **The shell game (bonneteau).** Three cups, a crowd of confederates who appear to be winning, and a game that cannot be won. Set up near Montmartre and along the Seine.
- **The friendship bracelet.** Tied onto your wrist near the Sacré-Cœur steps before you can withdraw your hand, then payment demanded.
- **Organised pickpocketing on the metro.** Concentrated on line 1 (Châtelet–La Défense), line 6 (Trocadéro–Nation), the RER B from CDG, and the Châtelet–Les Halles interchange.
- **Fake or resold attraction tickets.** In February 2026 French authorities arrested ten people, including Louvre employees, over a decade-long ticket-fraud scheme worth around €10 million that targeted tour groups.

None of these require you to be unlucky. They require you to stop moving.
sources: Common scams in Paris — France Hotel Guide

hidden_costs.body:
**The tourist tax (taxe de séjour) rose steeply on 1 January 2026** and is the single most common Paris billing surprise. It is charged per adult per night, on top of the room rate, and is usually collected at the property rather than by the booking site.

Paris rates in force from 1 January 2026:
- Palace: **€15.93** per adult per night
- 5-star: **€11.70**
- 3-star: **€5.53**
- Unclassified accommodation, including many short-term rentals: 5% of the nightly cost, capped at **€15.93**

Those figures include the Île-de-France Mobilités surcharge, which is levied at 200% of the base tax to fund regional transport. For a couple on a seven-night stay in a mid-range hotel, this is a line item in the tens of euros that appeared nowhere in the price you compared.

Other costs that are real but smaller: a single metro/RER ticket is **€2.55** (bus/tram €2.05), a day pass **€12.30**, and the tourist-branded Paris Visite pass runs from **€30.60** for one day — often worse value than the ordinary day pass unless you are travelling to the airport zones.
sources: Ville de Paris — taxe de séjour rates from 1 January 2026 (PDF)

transportation.body:
The metro is the right way to move around Paris, and it is also where most of the city's petty crime happens. Both things are true.

- **Buy from a machine or the RATP app, not from a person on the concourse.** Someone offering to help you at the machine is a recognised approach.
- **The RER B from Charles de Gaulle** is the cheapest airport connection and the one with the worst pickpocketing reputation, especially with luggage in the aisle at the doors.
- **A single ticket is €2.55; a day pass is €12.30.** Five or more journeys in a day means the day pass wins.
- **The Paris Visite pass is marketed at tourists and is frequently the worst value on offer** — it starts at €30.60 for one day. Compare it against a plain day pass before buying.
- **Strikes are announced in advance.** Check before a travel day rather than at the barrier.

closures.body:
**The Louvre is closed every Tuesday, all year, without exception**, plus 25 December, 1 January and 1 May. This is the most common single wasted day in Paris, and it is entirely avoidable.

Two other closure patterns matter and are less predictable:

- **Strikes.** The Louvre was closed to visitors by staff industrial action in December 2025. French strikes are normally announced a few days ahead; a non-refundable timed ticket does not survive one.
- **Heat.** In late June 2026 the Louvre announced 4pm closures from 24 to 27 June because of extreme heat, and Paris attractions including the Eiffel Tower have shortened hours in previous heat waves.

Before you buy a timed ticket, check the museum's own hours page for your exact date — not a third-party listing.
sources: Extreme heat forces early closure of Paris attractions — France 24

crowds.body:
Paris crowding is concentrated rather than general. The Louvre, the Eiffel Tower, Sacré-Cœur, Notre-Dame's exterior, Versailles and the Musée d'Orsay absorb most of it; a great deal of central Paris is comfortable even in August.

Practical consequences:
- **Timed entry sells out.** For the headline sights in summer, weeks ahead is normal, not cautious.
- **The queue you can see is not the queue you are in.** Security screening and ticket-holder entry are separate lines at several sights.
- **Versailles on a Tuesday** absorbs the Louvre's closed-day overflow.

neighborhoods.body:
Paris is small and well connected, so "central" matters less than it does in a sprawling city. What matters more is noise and what is directly outside the door.

- **Around the major stations** — Gare du Nord in particular — is convenient and markedly less pleasant at night than the price suggests.
- **Châtelet–Les Halles** is the most connected point in the city and also its busiest interchange, with the pickpocketing that follows from that.
- **Montmartre** is beautiful and steep. "Ten minutes from Sacré-Cœur" can mean ten minutes uphill with a suitcase.
- **The outer arrondissements are generally fine and much better value**, but check the walk from the metro at night rather than the straight-line distance on a map.

entry_requirements.body:
France is in the Schengen area. Requirements depend on your nationality and change; the only source worth trusting is your own government's travel advice page and the French government's own visa site, checked for your dates.

The items that most often catch people out are not visas but the surrounding paperwork: **passport validity rules** (many countries require validity beyond your return date rather than up to it), proof of accommodation, and proof of onward travel. Check these at least a month before you fly, not at the airport.

accommodation.body:
Two Paris-specific things to check before you confirm:

- **Is the tourist tax included?** Usually it is not. See the hidden-costs section for 2026 rates — for an unclassified short-term rental it can be up to €15.93 per adult per night.
- **Is there a lift?** Paris is a city of walk-ups. A fifth-floor apartment with no lift is a normal listing and a genuinely difficult one with luggage or limited mobility. Listings are inconsistent about saying so; ask.

faqs.q: How much is the Paris tourist tax in 2026?
faqs.a: It rose on 1 January 2026 and is charged per adult per night, usually collected at the property rather than by the booking site. Paris rates now run to €15.93 in a palace, €11.70 in a 5-star hotel, €5.53 in a 3-star, and 5% of the nightly cost capped at €15.93 for unclassified accommodation including many short-term rentals. Those figures include the Île-de-France Mobilités surcharge levied at 200% of the base tax.

faqs.q: Is the Louvre ever closed?
faqs.a: Yes — every Tuesday, all year round, plus 25 December, 1 January and 1 May. It has also closed or shortened hours for staff strikes (December 2025) and extreme heat (4pm closures from 24–27 June 2026). Check the museum's own hours page for your exact date before buying a timed ticket.

faqs.q: Where do pickpockets actually operate in Paris?
faqs.a: Reported activity is concentrated on metro line 1 (Châtelet–La Défense), line 6 (Trocadéro–Nation), the RER B from Charles de Gaulle airport, and the Châtelet–Les Halles interchange, plus the forecourts of the Eiffel Tower, Sacré-Cœur and the Louvre. The common approaches are distraction-based: a petition to sign, a shell game, or a bracelet tied onto your wrist.

faqs.q: Is the Paris Visite pass worth buying?
faqs.a: Usually not. It starts at €30.60 for one day, against €12.30 for an ordinary day pass and €2.55 for a single metro/RER ticket. It only makes sense if you are making several journeys into the outer airport zones on the same day. Compare it against a plain day pass for your actual itinerary before buying.

faqs.q: What is the worst time of year to visit Paris?
faqs.a: July and August combine the heaviest crowds, the highest heat risk and the French summer holiday, when a noticeable share of independent restaurants and shops close. Paris attractions have shortened hours during heat waves, including the Louvre's 4pm closures in late June 2026. April–May and late September–October are the windows where weather, crowds and prices are all reasonable at once.

pages.intro: Paris is not a dangerous city. It is an expensive one with several costs that are not in the price you compared, and a small number of closures that waste an entire day if you do not know about them.
pages.body:
Most ruined Paris trips come down to five things, and all five are checkable before you book.

**1. The tourist tax nobody quoted you.** Paris raised its taxe de séjour on 1 January 2026. It is charged per adult per night on top of the room rate and is normally collected at the property, so it does not appear in the total you used to compare hotels. Current rates run to €15.93 a night in a palace, €11.70 in a 5-star, €5.53 in a 3-star, and 5% of the nightly cost capped at €15.93 for unclassified accommodation — which includes a large share of short-term rentals. Those figures include the Île-de-France Mobilités surcharge, levied at 200% of the base tax to fund regional transport. For two people over a week this is not a rounding error.

**2. The Louvre is closed on Tuesdays.** Every Tuesday, all year, without exception, plus 25 December, 1 January and 1 May. This is the single most common wasted day in Paris. It also has knock-on effects: Versailles and the Musée d'Orsay absorb the overflow, so Tuesday is the worst day to substitute them in.

**3. Strikes and heat close things at short notice.** The Louvre was shut by staff industrial action in December 2025. In late June 2026 it announced 4pm closures for four consecutive days during a heat wave. French strikes are usually announced a few days ahead; heat closures are announced the day before or the morning of. A non-refundable timed ticket survives neither. Check the attraction's own hours page for your exact date.

**4. Pickpocketing, in specific places.** This is distraction crime, not violent crime, and it clusters: metro line 1 between Châtelet and La Défense, line 6 between Trocadéro and Nation, the RER B in from Charles de Gaulle, and the Châtelet–Les Halles interchange. On the street the approaches are a petition to sign, a shell game you cannot win, and a friendship bracelet tied onto your wrist before you can pull away. The common factor is that you stop moving and your attention goes somewhere other than your bag.

**5. Tickets bought from the wrong place.** Lookalike ticket sites resell entry at a markup, and the problem is not only unofficial: in February 2026 French authorities arrested ten people, including Louvre employees, over a ticket-fraud scheme worth around €10 million that ran for a decade against tour groups. Buy from the museum's own domain.

**What actually helps.** Move your dates out of July and August if you can — April to May and late September to October give you better weather, smaller queues and lower prices simultaneously. Buy the headline sights weeks ahead. Use an ordinary €12.30 day pass rather than the tourist-branded Paris Visite pass, which starts at €30.60 and is rarely the better deal. And ask your accommodation what the tourist tax will be before you book, not at checkout.
sources: Ville de Paris — taxe de séjour rates from 1 January 2026 (PDF)
Extreme heat forces early closure of Paris attractions — France 24

pages.meta_description: The petition, the shell game, the friendship bracelet and the metro lines where organised pickpocketing concentrates — and how to walk past all of them.
pages.intro: Almost every Paris scam works the same way: it makes you stop walking and look at something other than your bag. Recognising the opening is the whole defence.
pages.body:
**The petition.** Someone, usually presenting as a student or a charity volunteer, approaches with a clipboard and asks you to sign a petition — often for a disability charity. While you are reading, a second person works your pocket or bag. If you sign, you are then pressured for a donation. This runs on the Eiffel Tower forecourt, the Louvre approaches and around Sacré-Cœur. There is no version of this that is legitimate.

**The shell game (bonneteau).** Three cups or cards on a folding board, a dealer, and three or four people in the crowd who appear to be winning. They are part of it. The game is not winnable and the board folds away the instant police appear — which tells you what it is. Common along the Seine and near Montmartre.

**The friendship bracelet.** On the steps below Sacré-Cœur, someone takes your wrist and begins tying a woven bracelet before you can withdraw your hand, then asks for money and makes a scene if you decline. Keep your hands down and keep walking; this one is almost entirely defeated by not stopping.

**The dropped ring.** Someone "finds" a gold ring at your feet, offers it to you, then asks for money for it. The ring is brass.

**Organised pickpocketing on the metro.** This is the one that actually costs people phones and wallets, and it is concentrated on specific routes: line 1 between Châtelet and La Défense, line 6 between Trocadéro and Nation, the RER B in from Charles de Gaulle, and the Châtelet–Les Halles interchange. Teams work the doors at the moment they close. Luggage in the aisle marks you out on the airport run.

**Ticket fraud.** Lookalike sites resell attraction entry at a markup, and some sell tickets that do not work. This is not only an unofficial-website problem: in February 2026 French authorities arrested ten people, including Louvre employees, over a decade-long ticket-fraud scheme worth around €10 million aimed at tour groups. Buy from the attraction's own domain, and be suspicious of any "official" site whose contact details you cannot find.

**What actually works.** Keep moving when approached. Front pockets, or a bag worn across the body with the opening facing you, on lines 1 and 6 and the RER B. Do not put a phone on an outside café table. And if someone creates a small crisis around you — a spilled drink, a dropped object, a sudden crowd — that is the moment to check your bag rather than help.
sources: Common scams in Paris — France Hotel Guide

destinations.risk_summary:
Rome's failure modes are **tickets, driving and crowds**, in that order. The Colosseum ticketing market was so badly distorted by bulk-buying bots that Italy's competition authority fined the operators roughly €20 million; the historic-centre driving restrictions issue automatic fines by camera months after you have gone home; and the Jubilee year pushed visitor numbers to a level the city is still absorbing.

On top of that, from 2 February 2026 the lower basin of the Trevi Fountain moved to timed entry with a €2 charge.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes, unreservedly — with the caveat that Rome rewards booking further ahead than feels necessary and punishes renting a car more than almost any city in Europe.

If you are choosing dates, the Jubilee (24 December 2024 – 6 January 2026) drew an estimated additional 15 million visitors and its effects on pricing and availability have not fully unwound. Shoulder season is worth more here than usual.
destinations.worst_months: July–August (heat and crowds), major religious holidays

overview.body:
Rome packs an extraordinary density of major sights into a walkable centre that was never designed for the number of people now walking through it. The city's responses — timed entry, access charges, restricted driving zones — are mostly sensible, and mostly invisible until they cost you money.

The practical read: book the big sights early from official sources, do not drive into the centre, and treat any "skip the line" offer with suspicion until you have checked who is selling it.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes. Rome is one of the few cities where the famous things genuinely are the best things, so the crowd problem cannot be dodged by going somewhere else in the city.

What you can control is timing. April and late September to October give you workable temperatures and a real reduction in queue length. July and August combine the worst heat with the worst crowds, and the walk between sights — which is most of what you do in Rome — is the part that becomes unpleasant.

top_risks.body:
- **Colosseum tickets.** Standard-price tickets have been persistently unavailable because of bulk automated buying; Italy's competition authority fined the operator and six tour operators around €20 million over it.
- **ZTL driving fines.** Automatic camera fines of roughly €80–€335, often arriving months later through your rental company, with an administration fee on top.
- **New access charges.** From 2 February 2026 the Trevi Fountain's lower basin has timed entry and a €2 per person fee.
- **The tourist tax**, €3–€7 per person per night, collected at the property.
- **Crowds.** The 2025 Jubilee was expected to bring around 15 million additional visitors.
- **Heat** in July and August, in a city you experience mostly on foot.

scams.body:
Rome's most expensive problem is not a street scam at all — it is the ticket market.

**Ticket resale and hoarding.** Italy's competition authority (AGCM) fined CoopCulture €7 million for failing to prevent automated bulk buying of Colosseum tickets and for reserving a large share for its own guided-tour packages, causing "substantial and prolonged unavailability" of standard-priced tickets. Six tour operators were fined for using bots to buy tickets in bulk and reselling them bundled with services at much higher prices. Total fines came to roughly €20 million.

What that means for you: if the official site shows nothing available and a third-party site shows plenty at three times the price, that is the mechanism working as designed, not your bad luck.

**Lookalike ticket sites.** Fraudulent sites imitate official platforms closely. Check for real contact details and customer-support information before paying; a site that cannot be contacted is not a ticket seller.

**Street approaches.** The usual repertoire operates around Termini, the Colosseum and the Trevi Fountain: gladiator photos with a fee demanded afterwards, bracelet-tying, and "helpful" people at ticket machines. All are avoided by not stopping.
sources: Italy fines tour operators over Colosseum ticket hoarding
Italy fines Colosseum ticketing agencies over tourist pricing

hidden_costs.body:
- **Tourist tax (imposta di soggiorno):** roughly **€3–€7 per person per night**, depending on accommodation category. Collected at the property, usually in cash, and normally not included in the booking total.
- **Trevi Fountain lower basin:** from **2 February 2026**, time-reserved entry with a **€2 per person** charge, introduced to manage visitor flow.
- **ZTL fines:** **€80–€335** per violation. See the transport section — this is the largest avoidable cost in Rome.
- **Restaurant cover charges (coperto) and service.** Legitimate and normal, but they are on the bill rather than the menu board.
- **Bundled "skip the line" tours** sold at a large markup because standard tickets are unavailable — a direct consequence of the ticket-hoarding problem above.
sources: Tourist tax in Italy 2026: city rules and rates

transportation.body:
**Do not drive into central Rome.** This is the single most expensive avoidable mistake visitors make in Italy.

The historic centre is a ZTL (zona a traffico limitato) enforced by automatic cameras. Fines run **€80–€335** per violation, and because each camera is a separate offence, one wrong turn can generate several. They arrive months later via your rental company, which adds its own administration fee for identifying you. In 2026 Rome's ZTL was extended further, reaching the Colosseum area, and the historic-centre zone operates roughly 06:30–18:00 on weekdays and 14:00–18:00 on Saturdays.

A hotel inside the ZTL can register your plate — but only if you give them the details, and only for the window they register. "My hotel is in there" is not by itself a defence.

The rest is straightforward: the centre is walkable, the metro is limited but useful, and taxis should be taken from ranks.
sources: Rome ZTL 2026: map, fines and how to avoid tickets
Italy ZTL zones 2026 — driving bans in Rome, Florence and Milan

crowds.body:
The 2025 Jubilee year ran from 24 December 2024 to 6 January 2026 and was expected to bring around **15 million additional visitors** to Rome. The pressure that created on tickets, accommodation and the major basilicas has not fully unwound.

Practical consequences: book the Colosseum, the Vatican Museums and the Borghese Gallery as far ahead as your dates allow; expect the Trevi Fountain's lower basin to require a timed slot; and treat any same-day plan for a headline sight in summer as optimistic.
sources: Rome 2025: tourist tax, Jubilee preparations and monument access

closures.body:
Rome's closure risk is less about fixed weekly closing days than about religious calendar events and restoration.

- **Major religious dates** close or heavily restrict the basilicas and fill the centre.
- **Restoration scaffolding** moves around the major monuments continuously. It is rarely announced on booking pages. Search recent photographs of the specific monument before buying a timed ticket if seeing it uncovered matters to you.
- **August** sees a noticeable share of independent restaurants and shops close for the Italian summer holiday.

neighborhoods.body:
- **Around Termini station** is the cheapest central accommodation and the least pleasant at night. It is well connected and not dangerous by day; the gap between the price and the experience is what surprises people.
- **The historic centre** is where you want to be and is priced accordingly. Check whether the address is inside the ZTL if you are arriving by car — see the transport section.
- **Trastevere** is the standard recommendation and is genuinely good, but the streets around the nightlife are loud until very late. "Heart of Trastevere" in a listing is a noise warning.
- **Anywhere "10 minutes from the Colosseum"** should be checked on a map for what those ten minutes cross.

entry_requirements.body:
Italy is in the Schengen area; requirements depend on your nationality and change. Check your own government's advice and the Italian consular pages for your dates.

As elsewhere in Europe, the paperwork that catches people out is passport validity rules rather than visas. Many countries require validity for a period beyond your intended departure, not merely through it. Check a month ahead.

accommodation.body:
Two things to confirm in writing before booking:

- **The tourist tax** (€3–€7 per person per night) and whether it is cash-only at checkout. Many small properties still are.
- **Whether the address is inside the ZTL**, if you are arriving by car, and whether the property will register your plate for the specific dates and times you will drive in. An unregistered entry is an automatic fine per camera.

faqs.q: Why can't I get standard-price Colosseum tickets?
faqs.a: Because the market for them was distorted by automated bulk buying. Italy's competition authority fined the ticket operator CoopCulture €7 million for failing to prevent bot-driven hoarding and for reserving a large share of tickets for its own guided-tour packages, causing prolonged unavailability of standard-priced entry. Six tour operators were also fined for using bots to buy in bulk and reselling the tickets bundled with services at much higher prices — roughly €20 million in total. Book from the official site the moment your dates are fixed.

faqs.q: How much is the tourist tax in Rome?
faqs.a: Roughly €3–€7 per person per night depending on the accommodation category. It is collected at the property, often in cash, and is normally not part of the total shown when you book.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay to see the Trevi Fountain now?
faqs.a: To stand at the lower basin, yes. From 2 February 2026 Rome introduced time-reserved entry to the lower basin area with a €2 per person charge, to manage visitor flow. Viewing the fountain from the square is unaffected.

faqs.q: What happens if I drive into Rome's ZTL by accident?
faqs.a: A camera photographs your plate and a fine of roughly €80–€335 is issued automatically. Each camera you pass is a separate offence, so one wrong turn can produce several. The fine typically reaches you months later through your rental company, which adds an administration fee for identifying you. Rome extended its ZTL in 2026 to reach the Colosseum area; the historic-centre zone operates roughly 06:30–18:00 weekdays and 14:00–18:00 Saturdays.

pages.title_tag: Rome Transportation Mistakes That Cost Tourists Money
pages.meta_description: Rome's ZTL cameras issue automatic fines of EUR 80-335 that reach you months later via your rental company. The driving mistakes that cost visitors most.
pages.intro: The most expensive mistake a visitor makes in Rome is usually made in a rental car, in the first ten minutes, without noticing.
pages.body:
**The ZTL is the big one.** Rome's historic centre is a zona a traffico limitato — a restricted traffic zone enforced by automatic number-plate cameras. Driving into it without authorisation produces a fine of roughly €80 to €335. Each camera is a separate offence, so a single wrong turn through the centre can generate several fines at once.

What makes this worse than an ordinary parking ticket is the delay. The fine is issued to the registered keeper, which for a rental is the rental company. They identify you, add their own administration fee for doing so, and the paperwork reaches you months after you got home — often after you have forgotten the route you took. By then contesting it is difficult.

In 2026 Rome extended the ZTL further, reaching the Colosseum area. The historic-centre zone operates roughly 06:30–18:00 on weekdays and 14:00–18:00 on Saturdays, but hours vary by sub-zone and change, so the operating times are not something to memorise once and rely on.

**"My hotel is inside the ZTL" is not a defence by itself.** Hotels inside the zone can register a guest's plate with the authorities, but only if you give them the plate details, and only for the specific window they register. If you drive in the night before your registration starts, or drive back out two days after it ends, that is a fine. Get the confirmation in writing and check the dates.

**The simplest fix is not to rent a car at all.** Central Rome is walkable, and almost everything a visitor wants is inside or near the restricted zone. If you need a car for the wider region, collect it on the day you leave the city, from a location outside the centre, and return it the same way.

**Taxis.** Take them from official ranks or book them. Agree that the meter is running before the boot is opened. Fixed airport fares to the centre exist and are published; a driver quoting well above the published fixed fare is not offering you a service.

**Public transport.** The metro is limited — two main lines and a third — but it covers several of the sights well and is cheap. Validate your ticket. Buses are more comprehensive and slower. Neither has the pickpocketing profile of the Paris metro, but Termini station and the routes to the Vatican are the exceptions.

**Airport connections.** The Leonardo Express from Fiumicino to Termini is the fastest and simplest; regional trains are cheaper and slower. Both are better than a car you then have to park.
sources: Rome ZTL 2026: map, fines and how to avoid tickets
Italy ZTL zones 2026 — driving bans in Rome, Florence and Milan

destinations.risk_summary:
Barcelona is the clearest case in Europe of a city **actively pricing tourism down**, and the traveller pays for that in fees rather than in friction. In April 2026 the city raised its nightly accommodation levy to roughly **$10–$17 a night** for hotels and about **$14** for holiday rentals — among the highest in Europe — and cruise passengers on short calls face combined charges reaching **€30**.

Add Gaudí's centenary year, which is drawing extra demand to exactly the sights that were already the most oversubscribed, and the practical picture is: book earlier than you think, and budget for the levy.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes. Barcelona's problem is not that it has stopped being good; it is that it is the most oversubscribed it has ever been in a year when the Sagrada Família is reaching its most significant construction milestone in 144 years.

If you want the headline sights, treat tickets as the first thing you book, not the last. If you are flexible, the city outside the Gaudí circuit is far less pressured and considerably cheaper.
destinations.worst_months: July–August, and any week with several cruise calls

overview.body:
Barcelona has spent since 2024 deliberately reducing tourism pressure through pricing and regulation, after sustained resident protest about housing costs and crowding. For a visitor that means higher, more visible charges and more enforcement — more civic wardens at the Sagrada Família and Park Güell, tighter rental rules, and a levy that keeps rising.

The city is still excellent. It is simply no longer cheap, and no longer a place where you can turn up and buy a ticket on the day.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes, with the caveat that 2026 is a peak-demand year: it marks 100 years since Gaudí's death, and the Sagrada Família's Tower of Jesus Christ has just reached its full height of 172.5 metres, the biggest construction milestone in the basilica's history.

That is a genuine reason to go and a guarantee that everyone else has the same idea. Shoulder season is worth more here than in almost any other European city.

top_risks.body:
- **The accommodation levy**, raised in April 2026 to roughly $10–$17 per night for hotels and about $14 for holiday rentals.
- **Cruise-passenger charges** reaching a combined €30 for calls under 12 hours.
- **Centenary-year demand** on the Gaudí sights, plus a temporary surcharge of €2–5 from mid-2026.
- **Pickpocketing**, concentrated on Las Ramblas, the metro and the beach.
- **Sold-out timed entry** at the Sagrada Família and Park Güell, weeks ahead in summer.
- **August heat** in a city you walk.

hidden_costs.body:
Barcelona's charges are layered, and only some of them appear at booking.

- **Accommodation levy:** raised in April 2026 to roughly **$10–$17 per night** in hotels and about **$14 per night** for holiday rentals — among the highest in Europe. It combines a Catalan regional tax with a city surcharge, and is normally collected at the property.
- **Cruise passengers:** the city has moved to roughly double the per-person charge on overnight docking, and passengers spending under 12 hours in the city can face combined taxes of up to **€30**.
- **Gaudí centenary surcharge:** a temporary **€2–5** applies from mid-2026 on affected attractions.

For a week in a hotel, the levy alone is a three-figure line item for two people that was not in the rate you compared.
sources: Barcelona raises taxes to address overtourism

crowds.body:
2026 is Gaudí's centenary year and the Sagrada Família has just topped out its tallest tower at 172.5 metres. Demand at the Gaudí sights is correspondingly extreme.

The city has increased civic-warden patrols at the Sagrada Família and Park Güell specifically because of crowd pressure. Practically: timed entry to both sells out weeks ahead in summer, and "we'll get tickets when we arrive" is not a plan that works here any more.
sources: Barcelona travel guide — Gaudí centenary year

scams.body:
Barcelona's reputation for pickpocketing is earned, and it is overwhelmingly non-violent, distraction-based theft rather than robbery.

The recurring settings are Las Ramblas and the streets running off it, the metro (especially the airport and Sagrada Família lines), the beach — where bags left on towels disappear while people swim — and crowded restaurant terraces where a phone or bag on a chair is taken from behind.

The common approaches are the same family as elsewhere: a spilled drink, a dropped object, a sudden helpful stranger, a group closing around you at a metro door. The defence is boring and effective: nothing in a back pocket, nothing on a table, bag across the body with the opening in front.

neighborhoods.body:
- **Las Ramblas** is where visitors are told to stay and is the single most pickpocketed street in the city. It is also loud until very late.
- **The Gothic Quarter and El Raval** are atmospheric and adjacent; El Raval varies sharply street by street in a way a map does not convey.
- **Barceloneta** puts you on the beach and in the middle of the noise complaints that helped drive the city's tourism crackdown.
- **Eixample and Gràcia** are quieter, better value, and a short metro ride from everything. For most visitors this is the better trade.

Check holiday-rental listings carefully: Barcelona has been tightening short-term rental regulation, and an unlicensed listing can be cancelled.

transportation.body:
The metro is fast, cheap and the sensible way to move. Multi-journey travel cards beat single tickets quickly.

The two mistakes that cost visitors: taking an unofficial "taxi" from outside the airport terminal rather than the official rank, and assuming the airport metro/train fare is covered by a standard city travel card — airport zones are frequently a separate fare. Check before you tap.

weather.body:
July and August are hot and humid, and Barcelona is a city you experience on foot and in queues. The heat compounds the crowd problem rather than sitting beside it: a 40-minute wait at Park Güell in May is not the same experience in August.

May and late September to October give you swimmable sea, workable temperatures and materially shorter queues.

entry_requirements.body:
Spain is in the Schengen area. Requirements depend on your nationality and change; check your own government's advice and Spanish consular guidance for your dates.

As across Europe, the recurring problem is passport validity rules rather than visas — many countries require validity beyond your return date, not merely through it.

accommodation.body:
Two Barcelona-specific checks:

- **Is the nightly levy included in the total?** Usually not. At roughly $10–$17 per person per night for hotels it is a substantial addition over a week.
- **Is a holiday rental licensed?** Barcelona has been actively restricting short-term rentals as part of its overtourism response. An unlicensed listing is a cancellation risk, not merely a legal abstraction.

faqs.q: How much is Barcelona's tourist tax in 2026?
faqs.a: In April 2026 the city raised it to roughly $10–$17 per night for hotels and about $14 per night for holiday rentals — among the highest in Europe. It combines a Catalan regional tax with a city surcharge and is normally collected at the property rather than at booking. Cruise passengers spending under 12 hours in the city can face combined charges of up to €30.

faqs.q: Why is Barcelona so busy in 2026?
faqs.a: 2026 marks 100 years since Antoni Gaudí's death, and the Sagrada Família's Tower of Jesus Christ has just reached its full height of 172.5 metres — the most significant construction milestone in the basilica's 144-year history. That has concentrated additional demand on exactly the sights that were already the most oversubscribed.

faqs.q: Where does pickpocketing actually happen in Barcelona?
faqs.a: Overwhelmingly on and around Las Ramblas, on the metro (particularly the airport and Sagrada Família routes), on the beach where bags are left on towels, and at crowded restaurant terraces. It is distraction theft rather than robbery: nothing in a back pocket, nothing on a table, and a bag worn across the body defeats most of it.

destinations.risk_summary:
Amsterdam is now **the most heavily taxed city stay in Europe**, and most visitors do not find out until checkout. The tourist tax is **12.5% of the accommodation price**, and from 1 January 2026 Dutch VAT on hotel accommodation jumped from 9% to 21% — a combined tax burden of roughly **33.5%** on a room.

The city has said it intends to keep going: a proposed rise to 16% next year, then one point a year to 20% by 2030.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes, but go in with the real number. A €200 room is not a €200 room here; with 12.5% tourist tax and 21% VAT the effective rate is closer to €267.

Amsterdam is also genuinely crowded — 23.7 million tourist overnight stays in 2025, about 800,000 more than 2024 and well above the city's own target of under 20 million. Everything the city is doing is aimed at reducing that number, and the tool it is using is your bill.
destinations.worst_months: July–August, King's Day, tulip-season weekends

overview.body:
Amsterdam's risk profile is unusual: it is not really about crime or closures, it is about cost and density. The city has explicitly decided that it has too many visitors and is using taxation to reduce them, which means the gap between the price you compare and the price you pay is wider here than almost anywhere.

The second-order effect is crowding in a small centre built on canals, where the physical capacity of the streets is genuinely fixed.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes — with the caveat that Amsterdam rewards staying longer in fewer places and punishes a two-day dash through the centre in August.

If your interest is the major museums, they are excellent and timed entry works well. If your interest is atmosphere, the centre in peak season is not where you will find it; the outer canal ring and the neighbourhoods east and west of it are.

top_risks.body:
- **The tax stack.** 12.5% tourist tax plus 21% VAT from 1 January 2026 — roughly 33.5% on top of the room.
- **Cruise day charge** of €15 per passenger in 2026.
- **Crowding.** 23.7 million overnight stays in 2025 against a city target of under 20 million.
- **Bicycles.** The most common visitor injury here is being hit by a bike while standing in a cycle lane.
- **Sold-out museum slots** at the Rijksmuseum, Van Gogh Museum and Anne Frank House.
- **Rising taxes ahead** — a proposed 16% next year, rising to 20% by 2030.

hidden_costs.body:
Amsterdam's headline problem is the tax stack, and it is the largest in Europe.

- **Tourist tax: 12.5% of the accommodation price** (excluding VAT and the tourist tax itself). Already the highest tourism tax in Europe.
- **VAT on hotel accommodation rose from 9% to 21% on 1 January 2026.** Combined with the tourist tax, the total tax burden on a room is around **33.5%**.
- **Cruise passengers:** a day tourist tax of **€15 per passenger** in 2026.

The city's coalition has published plans to raise the tourist tax from 12.5% to **16% next year**, then by one percentage point annually to **20% in 2030**. If you are booking a future trip, budget on the higher number.

Check whether your booking total includes both taxes. Many international booking sites show the room net of one or both.
sources: Amsterdam proposes tourism tax hike to 20% — Skift
Amsterdam tourist tax 2026: rates and calculator

crowds.body:
Amsterdam recorded **23.7 million tourist overnight stays in 2025**, roughly 800,000 more than 2024, and well above the city's stated target of keeping annual overnight stays below 20 million.

That is the context for every measure the city has taken. Practically: the central canal ring, the Red Light District and the museum quarter are the pressure points; timed entry at the major museums sells out; and the physical width of the streets means crowding is felt more sharply than the raw numbers suggest.
sources: Amsterdam tourist tax may rise as overnight stays hit 23.7m

transportation.body:
**Bicycles are traffic, not decoration.** The most common way a visitor gets hurt in Amsterdam is by standing in, or stepping into, a cycle lane. Cycle lanes are usually the reddish strip between the pavement and the road; cyclists have priority and travel faster than they look.

If you rent a bike, you are joining that traffic with its rules, at its speed, on the first day. Many visitors are better off on trams.

From Schiphol, the train to Amsterdam Centraal is fast, frequent and cheap; it is almost always the right choice over a taxi.

scams.body:
Amsterdam is not a scam-heavy city by European standards. The recurring problems are ordinary pickpocketing in the crowded central streets and on trams, aggressive touting around the Red Light District, and fake or overpriced "tour" tickets sold on the street near Centraal.

Buy museum and canal tickets from the operator's own site. Anyone selling attraction entry on the pavement is not the operator.

neighborhoods.body:
- **The Red Light District and the streets immediately around it** are loud all night and are the focus of the city's nuisance enforcement. A cheap central room here is cheap for a reason.
- **The central canal ring** is beautiful and the most crowded part of the city in daylight.
- **De Pijp, Oud-West and the Eastern Docklands** are quieter, better value, and 10–20 minutes by tram from the centre.

One practical Amsterdam-specific check: canal houses are old and steep. "Second floor" can mean a near-ladder staircase with no lift, which matters with luggage.

entry_requirements.body: The Netherlands is in the Schengen area; requirements depend on nationality and change. Check your own government's travel advice and Dutch consular guidance for your dates, paying particular attention to passport validity rules rather than visa rules.

accommodation.body:
The single most important thing to confirm is **which taxes your quoted total already includes**. With 12.5% tourist tax and 21% VAT since 1 January 2026, a booking shown net of both is roughly a third cheaper than the amount you will actually pay.

Ask the property for the all-in total in writing before you commit, especially for longer stays where the difference runs into hundreds of euros.

faqs.q: How much tax will I actually pay on an Amsterdam hotel room?
faqs.a: Around 33.5% on top of the room price. The tourist tax is 12.5% of the accommodation price — already the highest in Europe — and Dutch VAT on hotel accommodation rose from 9% to 21% on 1 January 2026. Check whether your booking total includes both; many international sites show the room net of one or both.

faqs.q: Is Amsterdam's tourist tax going up again?
faqs.a: The city's coalition has published plans to raise it from 12.5% to 16% next year, then by one percentage point each year until it reaches 20% in 2030. If you are booking a trip for a future year, budget on the higher figure.

faqs.q: What is the most common way visitors get hurt in Amsterdam?
faqs.a: Being hit by a bicycle after standing in or stepping into a cycle lane. Cycle lanes are usually the reddish strip between the pavement and the road, cyclists have priority, and they travel faster than they appear to. It is the single most avoidable injury risk in the city.

destinations.risk_summary:
Los Angeles ruins trips through **distance and billing**, not danger. The city is roughly the size of a small country and the gap between two things on your list is frequently an hour each way, which is how a five-day trip becomes two days of sightseeing and three days of driving.

On top of that, the city's transient occupancy tax is **14%**, hotels covered by the tourism marketing district add a further **2%** of room revenue, and resort fees at some properties add **$20–$30 a night** or around 10% of the rate.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes, if you plan it geographically rather than by attraction list. Pick two or three areas and stay near them; do not try to "do LA" from one hotel.

The common regret here is not that the city disappointed but that the itinerary was built from a map that made everything look adjacent. Santa Monica to Downtown at 5pm is a different trip from the same distance at 10am.
destinations.worst_months: Late summer (heat and wildfire smoke risk), any weekday rush hour

overview.body:
Los Angeles is a set of distinct cities that share an airport. Almost every practical problem a visitor has here traces back to that: the drive times, the parking costs, the decision about where to stay, and the discovery that the "nearby" beach is 40 minutes away in good traffic.

Crime is not the main story for most visitors. Vehicle break-ins and property theft are the realistic risks, and they are concentrated where visitors park.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes — but plan by geography. The most useful decision you will make is which two or three areas you actually care about (beaches, Hollywood/Griffith, Downtown, Pasadena, Santa Monica/Venice) and staying in or between them.

A visitor staying downtown and doing a beach day, a theme park day and a Hollywood day will spend most of the trip on the 110 and the 405.

top_risks.body:
- **Drive times.** Distances that look short are not, and rush hour roughly doubles them.
- **The tax and fee stack.** 14% city transient occupancy tax, up to 2% tourism-district charge, plus resort fees of $20–$30 a night at some properties.
- **Parking.** Frequently $20–$60 a day at hotels and attractions, rarely quoted at booking.
- **Vehicle break-ins** at trailheads, beach lots and tourist parking.
- **Booking the wrong airport.** LAX, Burbank, Long Beach, John Wayne and Ontario are not interchangeable once you see the drive.
- **Heat and wildfire smoke** in late summer.

hidden_costs.body:
- **Transient occupancy tax: 14%** on the room in the City of Los Angeles.
- **Tourism marketing district assessment:** covered hotels charge **2%** of room rental revenue (raised from 1.5% effective 1 May 2022).
- **A further 2% hotel tax** was placed on the June 2026 ballot by the City Council, tied to the 2028 Olympics budget plan — check the current rate for your dates.
- **Resort fees:** roughly **$20–$30 a night** at some beach properties, and at some hotels around **10% of the published room rate**.
- **Parking** at hotels and attractions, commonly $20–$60 a day, plus per-park theme park parking.

Typical daily costs in 2026 run roughly $80–$130 per person budget, $185–$270 mid-range and $405–$640 luxury — before the room.
sources: US hotel stays cost more as bed taxes climb

transportation.body:
This is where LA trips are won or lost.

- **Rush hour roughly doubles every drive.** Roughly 06:30–10:00 and 15:00–19:30 on weekdays, worse on Fridays.
- **Rideshare adds up fast** across a city this size; three cross-town trips a day is a meaningful daily cost.
- **Parking is a separate budget line**, not an afterthought — hotel parking is frequently $20–$60 a day and is rarely in the quoted rate.
- **The Metro is genuinely useful along its lines** (particularly Downtown, Hollywood, Santa Monica and Long Beach) and useless everywhere else. Check whether your two anchors are actually on it before assuming you can skip a car.
- **Never leave anything visible in a parked car**, especially at trailheads, beach lots and viewpoint parking. This is the most common property crime against visitors.

airport.body:
Los Angeles has five airports a visitor might reasonably fly into, and choosing the cheapest fare without checking the drive is a classic mistake.

- **LAX** is the biggest and the most congested; allow far more time than the distance suggests, and be aware that curbside pickup arrangements for rideshare have changed repeatedly — check the current rule before you land.
- **Burbank (BUR)** is small, pleasant and much closer to Hollywood, Pasadena and the valley.
- **Long Beach (LGB)** and **John Wayne (SNA)** serve the south and Orange County well.
- **Ontario (ONT)** is a long way east of the city.

A $60 cheaper fare into the wrong airport can cost more than that in the transfer, twice.

neighborhoods.body:
"Is downtown LA safe?" is the most asked question about this city, and the honest answer is that it varies sharply within a few blocks and by time of day. The Financial District and the areas around the arena and the arts district are ordinary; a few blocks east is one of the largest concentrations of street homelessness in the United States, and it is not a place to wander at night.

More practically for most visitors: staying downtown puts you far from the beaches, and staying at the beach puts you far from everything else. Choose the trade deliberately rather than by hotel price.

weather.body:
The climate is the reason people come and is rarely the problem. Two things to plan around:

- **Late-summer heat inland.** The coast stays moderate; the valley does not.
- **Wildfire smoke.** Air quality can deteriorate sharply and at short notice in late summer and autumn, and it affects outdoor plans across the basin regardless of where the fire is.

"June gloom" — a persistent coastal marine layer in late spring — regularly disappoints people who booked a beach trip for early June.

crowds.body:
Los Angeles absorbs visitors better than a compact European city, so general crowding is not the problem. Specific choke points are: theme parks in school holidays, the Griffith Observatory at sunset (parking is the constraint, not the building), and the Santa Monica and Venice beachfront at summer weekends.

Event traffic is the bigger effect. A concert or a game near your route can add an hour without warning.

entry_requirements.body:
For international visitors the United States requires either a visa or, for eligible nationalities, an approved **ESTA** obtained in advance — not on arrival. Apply well before departure and only through the official government site; a large number of lookalike sites charge a substantial markup for the same application.

Check your own government's advice and the official US guidance for your nationality and dates.

accommodation.body:
Ask two questions before booking anything in Los Angeles:

1. **What is the resort or facility fee, and what is the parking charge?** Together these routinely add $40–$90 a night that is not in the quoted rate.
2. **What is actually within walking distance?** In most of this city the answer is "nothing", and that turns every evening into a driving decision.

faqs.q: What does a Los Angeles hotel actually cost after taxes and fees?
faqs.a: Considerably more than the quoted rate. The city transient occupancy tax is 14%, hotels in the tourism marketing district add 2% of room revenue, resort fees run $20–$30 a night at some beach properties (or around 10% of the rate), and parking is commonly a further $20–$60 a day. A further 2% hotel tax was placed on the June 2026 ballot tied to the 2028 Olympics budget plan, so check the current rate for your dates.

faqs.q: Which Los Angeles airport should I fly into?
faqs.a: Whichever is closest to where you are actually staying, not whichever is cheapest. LAX is the largest and most congested. Burbank is far more convenient for Hollywood, Pasadena and the valley. Long Beach and John Wayne serve the south and Orange County. Ontario is a long way east. A cheaper fare into the wrong airport is frequently more expensive once you pay for the transfer twice.

faqs.q: Is downtown Los Angeles safe for tourists?
faqs.a: It varies sharply within a few blocks and by time of day. The Financial District, the arena area and the Arts District are ordinary daytime environments; a few blocks east is one of the largest concentrations of street homelessness in the United States and is not a place to walk at night. The more common practical problem for visitors is not violence but vehicle break-ins — never leave anything visible in a parked car.

destinations.risk_summary:
Honolulu's risk is almost entirely **cost, and cost that arrives after you have booked**. From 1 January 2026 Hawaii's Green Fee added **0.75%** to the transient accommodations tax — the first climate impact fee of its kind in the United States — taking the combined lodging tax on Oahu from roughly 18.0% to about **18.7%**, before any resort fee.

On top of that, resort fees and parking in Waikiki are close to universal, and a rental car you keep for the whole trip is usually a large avoidable expense.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes. Oahu is not a place people regret going; it is a place people regret budgeting for badly.

The two decisions that matter are how many days you actually need a car (usually fewer than you booked) and whether the resort fee buys anything you will use. Get those right and the trip works.
destinations.worst_months: Late December–early January, mid-June–August (price peaks)

overview.body:
Honolulu is a straightforward destination with an unusually complicated bill. Nothing here is trying to catch you out — the taxes are published and the fees are disclosed somewhere — but the number of separate charges means the difference between the rate you compared and the amount you pay is larger than most US cities.

The practical risks beyond cost are ocean conditions and sun, both of which are managed by paying attention rather than by planning.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes. The regret pattern here is financial rather than experiential: people arrive having budgeted the room rate and find the room costs roughly a quarter more once tax and resort fee land, then add parking they had not counted.

Budget the all-in nightly figure from the start and Honolulu stops being a surprise.

top_risks.body:
- **The Green Fee and the tax stack.** Roughly **18.7%** combined lodging tax on Oahu from January 2026.
- **Resort fees**, near-universal in Waikiki, plus **parking** which is separately charged and expensive.
- **Rental car costs and parking** for days you do not need one.
- **Ocean conditions.** Surf on the north shore in winter is not a beginner environment, and conditions change by beach and season.
- **Sun.** Reef-safe sunscreen rules apply and the UV index is high year-round.
- **Peak-season pricing** at Christmas–New Year and mid-summer.

hidden_costs.body:
**Hawaii's Green Fee took effect on 1 January 2026.** Act 96 (Senate Bill 1396), signed on 27 May 2025, created the first climate impact fee in the United States by raising the state transient accommodations tax by **0.75%**, to an 11% state rate. It is expected to raise around $100 million a year for climate and conservation work.

For a visitor the practical effect is:
- The combined lodging tax on Oahu — state TAT, county accommodations tax and general excise tax — rises from roughly **18.0% to about 18.7%**.
- That is roughly **$3 a night** on a typical Waikiki room.

A federal judge blocked one part of the law, the provision that would have applied an 11% tax to cruise-ship passenger bills; the accommodation portion is in force.

On top of the tax: **resort fees** are close to universal in Waikiki, and **parking is charged separately** and is expensive. Neither is normally in the compared rate.
sources: Hawaii Green Fee 2026: what visitors pay on a hotel stay
Court decision allows Hawaii's Green Fee to take full effect — KHON2
How to read an Oahu hotel rate in 2026

transportation.body:
Waikiki is walkable and well served by TheBus; much of Oahu is not.

The common expensive mistake is renting a car for the entire stay when you need it for two or three days. Hotel parking in Waikiki is charged nightly and is one of the larger line items on the bill, so a car that sits in a garage for four days costs twice — rental and parking.

Book the car for the days you are actually driving round the island.

weather.body:
Honolulu's weather is reliable; the ocean is not uniformly so.

- **North shore surf in winter** (roughly November to March) is world-class and genuinely dangerous for swimmers. It is a different environment from the south-shore beaches on the same island.
- **Conditions vary by beach and by day.** Lifeguarded beaches post warnings; they are worth reading rather than glancing at.
- **UV is high year round.** Hawaii restricts certain sunscreen chemicals, so bring or buy reef-safe products.
- **Hurricane season** runs roughly June to November; direct hits are rare but travel insurance is worth more in that window.

crowds.body:
Waikiki is dense and busy year-round, with sharp peaks over Christmas–New Year and in mid-summer, when both prices and beach density are at their highest.

Popular hikes — Diamond Head in particular — now use reservation systems for non-residents. Check and book before you drive there.

scams.body:
Honolulu is not a scam-heavy destination. The recurring issues are timeshare and "activity desk" presentations sold as free tours or discounted attractions, and third-party activity resellers charging above the operator's own price.

Book activities directly with the operator, and treat any offer that requires attending a presentation as costing you a half-day.

neighborhoods.body:
- **Waikiki** is where most visitors stay: convenient, walkable, busy, and where the resort fees and parking charges are concentrated.
- **Ko Olina and the west side** are quieter and resort-focused, and a long way from Honolulu proper.
- **The north shore** is a different trip entirely — rural, spread out, and requiring a car.

Staying outside Waikiki without a car is a mistake; staying in Waikiki with a car you rarely use is an expensive one.

entry_requirements.body:
Hawaii is a US state, so international visitors need the same visa or **ESTA** as for the mainland, obtained in advance. Apply only through the official government site — lookalike sites charge a large markup for the identical application.

Domestic US travellers should check current identification requirements for domestic flights well before departure.

accommodation.body:
Ask for the **all-in nightly total**, not the rate. On Oahu that means the room, roughly 18.7% combined lodging tax from January 2026, the resort fee, and parking if you will have a car.

Then ask what the resort fee actually includes. If it is beach towels and a Wi-Fi connection you would have had anyway, it is a rate increase with a different name — and it is worth comparing properties on the all-in figure rather than the headline.

faqs.q: What is Hawaii's Green Fee and how much does it add?
faqs.a: It is the first climate impact fee in the United States, created by Act 96 (Senate Bill 1396), signed 27 May 2025 and effective 1 January 2026. It raises the state transient accommodations tax by 0.75% to an 11% state rate, and is expected to generate around $100 million a year for climate and conservation work. For a visitor it adds roughly $3 a night, taking the combined lodging tax on Oahu from about 18.0% to about 18.7%.

faqs.q: Does the Green Fee apply to cruise passengers?
faqs.a: Not currently. A federal judge blocked the provision of the law that would have applied an 11% tax to cruise-ship passenger bills. The accommodation portion took effect on 1 January 2026 as planned.

faqs.q: Do I need a rental car for the whole stay in Honolulu?
faqs.a: Usually not. Waikiki is walkable and served by TheBus, and hotel parking is charged nightly and is expensive — so a car that sits in the garage costs you twice, in rental and in parking. Book it for the days you are actually driving around the island.

destinations.risk_summary:
San Francisco's reputation runs well behind its current reality, and both the alarm and the dismissal are wrong. Car break-ins are **down significantly since 2023** and falling further into 2026, tourism is back, and the main visitor areas are ordinary. But one specific area — roughly six blocks between Union Square and Civic Center — accounts for a **wildly disproportionate share of visitor incidents**, and a rental car with anything visible in it is still a target anywhere in the city.

On top of that, a **14% transient occupancy tax** adds $21–$34 a night to a typical mid-range room.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes. The honest framing is that San Francisco is a normal major city with one concentrated problem area and a property-crime pattern that is entirely avoidable with one habit: never leave anything visible in a parked car.

What surprises people more than crime is the weather. Summer in San Francisco is cold and foggy, and visitors regularly arrive in July dressed for California and spend the first afternoon buying a fleece.
destinations.worst_months: June–August (fog and cold, despite being peak season)

overview.body:
San Francisco is small, dense and walkable in a way most American cities are not, which makes it unusually rewarding — and means one bad block is genuinely adjacent to a good one.

The two things that most affect a visitor are the weather (colder and foggier in summer than almost anyone expects) and the decision about whether to have a car at all.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes. The city's reputation took a hard hit in 2020–2023 and has not fully recovered in the public mind, but by 2026 car break-ins are down significantly, downtown is busy again and tourism is strong.

The practical caveats are narrow and specific: one concentrated area to route around, one habit about parked cars, and warm clothes in July.

top_risks.body:
- **Vehicle break-ins.** Down substantially from the 2023 peak but still the most likely thing to happen to you. Anything visible, anywhere, is a target.
- **The Tenderloin**, roughly bounded by Market, Powell, Geary and Van Ness — a small area with a very large share of visitor incident reports.
- **The weather.** Summer is cold and foggy; this genuinely disrupts plans.
- **The 14% transient occupancy tax**, adding $21–$34 a night to a mid-range room.
- **Hills.** "Six blocks" can be a serious climb, which matters with luggage or limited mobility.
- **Parking costs and tickets**, which are aggressive.

neighborhoods.body:
This is the section that matters most in San Francisco, because the variation is sharp and the distances are short.

**The Tenderloin** sits between Union Square and Civic Center and presents visible street homelessness, open drug activity and aggressive panhandling, concentrated in roughly six blocks bounded by Market, Powell, Geary and Van Ness. Reporting puts it at around **31% of tourist-related crime reports despite being under 2% of the city's area**, and it carries the city's lowest neighbourhood safety score.

That is not an argument for fear — it is an argument for knowing where it is. A hotel advertised as "steps from Union Square" can be on the wrong side of that line, and the price will tell you before the listing does.

The main visitor areas — Fisherman's Wharf, Union Square proper, North Beach, the Valencia Street corridor in the Mission, and the Financial District — are ordinary daytime environments used by millions of visitors without incident.

hidden_costs.body:
- **Transient occupancy tax: 14%**, which on a typical mid-range room of $150–$240 adds roughly **$21–$34 a night**.
- **Parking.** Hotel parking downtown is expensive and often not included; street parking is metered aggressively and ticketed reliably.
- **Bridge tolls** are charged electronically and billed through rental companies with an administration fee.

The honest summary is that San Francisco is expensive rather than deceptive — the charges are visible, they are just large.

transportation.body:
**The single most useful rule in San Francisco: never leave anything visible in a parked car.** Smash-and-grab theft targets rental cars and visible valuables within minutes of parking, throughout the city including tourist areas. Break-ins are well down since 2023 and 2026 is running lower still, but this remains the most likely thing to happen to a visitor.

An empty-looking car is not enough — a charging cable or a bag-shaped object under a coat is a cue. Leave the boot genuinely empty.

Beyond that: the city is compact and Muni, BART and the cable cars cover most of what a visitor wants. Many trips here do not need a car at all, and not having one removes the risk entirely.

weather.body:
San Francisco's summer is the most commonly misjudged thing about the city. June to August is frequently cold, grey and windy, with fog that sits over the western half of the city for days. Visitors arrive in July dressed for California and spend the first afternoon buying warm clothing.

**September and October are the actual warm months.** If you can choose, choose those. If you cannot, pack layers and a windproof jacket regardless of the month, and expect the temperature to differ noticeably between the Mission and the coast on the same afternoon.

crowds.body: Crowding is not a major issue in San Francisco compared with European city centres. The pressure points are the cable car turnarounds, Alcatraz (which sells out well in advance — book it early, it is the one thing that genuinely requires planning), and Fisherman's Wharf on summer weekends.

scams.body:
San Francisco is not a scam-heavy city. The recurring issues are unofficial "tour" and Alcatraz ticket sellers near the waterfront — Alcatraz tickets sell out and the resale market is where people get caught — and aggressive street solicitation around Powell and Market.

Buy Alcatraz tickets from the official concessionaire, early.

entry_requirements.body:

Check your own government's advice and official US guidance for your nationality and dates.

accommodation.body:
Check the **exact address on a map** before booking anything advertised as near Union Square or Civic Center, and look at which streets you would walk between the hotel and the places you plan to go at night. A conspicuously cheap central room is usually cheap for a locational reason.

Also confirm the parking charge if you are driving, and whether the room rate is quoted before the 14% transient occupancy tax.

faqs.q: Is San Francisco safe for tourists in 2026?
faqs.a: For the main visitor areas, yes — Fisherman's Wharf, Union Square proper, North Beach, the Valencia Street corridor and the Financial District are ordinary daytime environments. faqs.a: They are the most likely thing to happen to a visitor, though the numbers are well down from the 2023 peak and 2026 is running lower still. Thieves target rental cars and visible valuables within minutes of parking, throughout the city. The rule that actually works is leaving nothing visible at all — including cables, empty bags and anything under a coat.

faqs.q: Why is San Francisco cold in summer?
faqs.a: Coastal fog. June to August is frequently cold, grey and windy, and the fog can sit over the western half of the city for days. September and October are the genuinely warm months. Visitors regularly arrive in July dressed for California weather and buy a fleece on the first afternoon.

Add a 4% city resort tax and a 3% county convention development tax on top of Florida's 6% sales tax, and the headline rate is a poor guide to the bill.
destinations.worth_visiting:

Spring break 2026 is also a materially different environment from recent years: the city has relaxed the emergency measures it used previously, with no blanket midnight curfew, beaches not closing at 6pm and parking garages reopening in the entertainment district.

overview.body:
Miami is a straightforward destination with an unusually volatile price structure. The variables that matter are the calendar — event weekends, spring break, high season — and the fee stack that sits on top of whatever the rate is.

The underlying risks beyond cost are weather (hurricane season is long) and the ordinary property-crime precautions of any busy beach city.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes. Miami rewards choosing your dates around the events calendar more than almost any US destination, because the same room can vary by several hundred dollars a night depending on what is on.

If your dates are fixed and land on a peak weekend, expect South Beach hotels to carry a 300–500% premium and budget chains to reach $400–$600 a night.

hidden_costs.body:

transportation.body:

scams.body:

neighborhoods.body:

A single Epic Universe day starts at **$139** for adults and rises to **$199** at peak dates near Christmas and New Year; a 3-day park-to-park ticket including Epic Universe starts around **$520.79**. None of that includes parking, food, express passes or hotel — and the families who run out of money here are almost always the ones who budgeted the gate price.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes, if you build the budget from the total rather than the ticket, and if you accept that a park day is a long, hot, crowded day that needs planning.

The biggest 2026 change is positive: park-to-park tickets now include Epic Universe on every day of a multi-day ticket, where previously multi-day tickets allowed only a single day there.
destinations.worst_months: Late December–early January, mid-June–August (heat, crowds and peak pricing)

overview.body:
Orlando is a destination where almost every problem is a budgeting or scheduling problem rather than a safety one. The parks are well run; they are also expensive, hot in summer, and structured so that the advertised entry price is a fraction of the day's cost.

The visitors who have a bad time are usually the ones who under-planned the days and under-budgeted everything that is not the ticket.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes — with the caveat that Orlando rewards fewer, better-planned park days over more rushed ones. Two well-run days usually beat four exhausted ones, and cost less.

If you are going for Epic Universe specifically, 2026 is a better year than 2025: multi-day park-to-park tickets now include it every day rather than once.

top_risks.body:
- **Ticket cost.** Epic Universe from **$139** a day, up to **$199** at Christmas/New Year peaks; multi-day park-to-park from around **$520.79**.
- **Everything that is not the ticket** — parking, food, express passes, hotel, transfers.
- **Summer heat and afternoon thunderstorms**, which regularly close outdoor rides.
- **Crowds** in school holidays, when queue times multiply.
- **Booking the wrong airport** — MCO and Sanford are not interchangeable.
- **Hurricane season**, June to November.

hidden_costs.body:
The gate price is the smallest number in an Orlando budget.

**2026 Universal ticket pricing:**
- Epic Universe single-day: from **$139** adult, up to **$199** at peak dates near Christmas and New Year; children 3–9 from **$134**.
- 3-day park-to-park (including Epic Universe): from about **$520.79**; 3-day base from about **$456.88**.
- Multi-day park hoppers work out from about **$105–$124 per day** depending on length.
- With tax, Epic Universe tickets run roughly **$273–$514** depending on date and ticket type.

**What is not in those figures:** theme-park parking (charged per park, per day), in-park food and drink for a full day, express/skip-the-line passes, hotel, and airport transfers. For a family of four, these routinely exceed the ticket cost.

Budget the whole day, not the entry.
