weather.body:
Central Florida summers are hot, extremely humid, and characterised by near-daily afternoon thunderstorms. Lightning closes outdoor rides and water parks routinely — not as an exception.

Plan outdoor attractions for the morning and indoor ones for mid-afternoon, and carry water. Heat exhaustion in queues is a genuine and common problem, particularly with children.

**Hurricane season runs 1 June to 30 November.** Orlando is inland, so the risk is disruption — flight cancellations, park closures — rather than direct danger.

transportation.body:
**Check which airport your fare is for.** Orlando International (MCO) is the main airport and the closest to the parks. Sanford (SFB) is used by low-cost carriers and is a materially longer drive. Tampa (TPA) is over an hour away.

Most visitors need a car or will pay repeatedly for transfers. Resort shuttle services exist and are slow; factor the time cost of a shuttle that runs on its own schedule against parking charges.

Theme-park parking is charged per park per day and is not included in any ticket.

scams.body:
Orlando's characteristic problem is **third-party ticket resale**. Discounted park tickets sold by roadside kiosks, timeshare presentations and unofficial sites are the recurring complaint: partially used tickets, tickets tied to a presentation you must attend, or tickets that simply do not scan.

Buy from the park operator or an authorised seller. A discount that requires attending a 90-minute presentation is not a discount, it is a purchase of your morning.

neighborhoods.body:
Orlando's accommodation decision is functional rather than about safety.

- **On-property park hotels** cost more and buy you early entry and transport.
- **International Drive** is central to several parks, busy, and full of mid-range options.
- **Kissimmee and the Highway 192 corridor** are cheaper and further out; the drive is real.
- **Vacation rentals** west of the parks are good value for families and require a car.

Check the actual drive time to the specific park you will visit most, in morning traffic.

entry_requirements.body:
International visitors need a US visa or, for eligible nationalities, an approved **ESTA** obtained in advance. Apply only via the official government site; lookalike sites charge a large markup for the identical application.

Check your own government's advice and official US guidance for your nationality and dates.

accommodation.body:
Check the **resort fee and the parking charge** before booking — both are common in Orlando and neither is usually in the compared rate.

For families, check what "sleeps 6" actually means: a sofa bed in a standard room is a very different week from two bedrooms, and the price difference is often smaller than the comfort difference over a seven-night stay.

faqs.q: How much do Epic Universe tickets cost in 2026?
faqs.a: Single-day adult tickets start at $139 and rise to $199 at peak dates near Christmas and New Year; children aged 3–9 start at $134. A 3-day park-to-park ticket including Epic Universe starts around $520.79, and a 3-day base ticket around $456.88. With tax, Epic Universe tickets run roughly $273–$514 depending on date and ticket type. None of that includes parking, food or express passes.

faqs.q: Can I visit Epic Universe on more than one day of a multi-day ticket?
faqs.a: Yes, as of 2026. Park-to-park tickets now include Epic Universe, and multi-day tickets allow access every day — previously multi-day tickets allowed only a single day there. That materially changes how to schedule a multi-day trip, since you no longer need to compress Epic Universe into one day.

faqs.q: Which Orlando airport should I fly into?
faqs.a: Orlando International (MCO) is the main airport and closest to the parks. Sanford (SFB) is used by low-cost carriers and is a materially longer drive. Tampa (TPA) is over an hour away. A cheaper fare into Sanford or Tampa can be wiped out by the transfer, especially for a family.

destinations.risk_summary:
London is expensive and busy but structurally forgiving — the things that ruin trips here are **fare mistakes and driving charges**, both of which are entirely avoidable.

The two numbers worth knowing: the **£8.90 daily cap** and **£44.70 Monday-to-Sunday cap** for Zones 1–2. Pay with the same card or phone every time and you cannot be overcharged. Switch between your phone and the physical card mid-day and your journeys stop counting toward the same cap — which is the single most common way visitors overpay.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes. London's risks are financial and logistical rather than dangerous, and almost all of them are solved by two habits: tap in and out with the same payment method every time, and do not drive.

The ULEZ now covers effectively all of Greater London inside the M25, which means a rental car is a daily charge before you have parked it.
destinations.worst_months: Late December (closures), any Tube strike day

overview.body:
London is one of the easier major cities to visit badly and still enjoy. The transport system is excellent and self-correcting if you use it properly; the accommodation is expensive but honest about it; the crowding is concentrated in a handful of places.

Where it catches people out is the fare system's edge cases and the vehicle charging zones, both of which cost money silently.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes. There is no version of a London trip that is ruined by London itself — only by a rental car, a forgotten tap-out, or an assumption that the West End theatre you wanted has seats this week.

Book theatre and the major exhibitions ahead; everything else is walk-up.

top_risks.body:
- **Mixing payment methods** across a day, which breaks the fare cap.
- **Forgetting to tap out** on rail services, which triggers a maximum fare.
- **Driving.** ULEZ now covers effectively all of Greater London inside the M25, and the Congestion Charge applies on top in the centre.
- **Buying an Oyster card you did not need** and leaving credit on it.
- **Strike days**, announced in advance.
- **Ordinary pickpocketing** in the West End and on packed Tube carriages.

hidden_costs.body:
London's transport pricing is generous if you use it correctly and punitive if you do not.

- **Zones 1–2 daily cap: £8.90.** Weekly (Monday–Sunday) cap for Zones 1–2: **£44.70.**
- **Contactless matches Oyster exactly** on fares and caps, with no £10 card fee, no deposit to reclaim and no leftover credit stranded on a card when you fly home. For most visitors the Oyster card is simply an unnecessary £10.
- **Use one payment method all day.** If you tap in with your phone and out with the physical card — even on the same bank account — the journeys may not count toward the same cap.
- **On rail services you must tap in AND out.** A missing tap-out triggers a maximum fare, which is several times the correct one.

For drivers: **ULEZ** now covers virtually all of Greater London within the M25 and is charged daily, with the central **Congestion Charge** on top inside the zone. A rental car in London is a running cost before it moves.

transportation.body:
**Use one card or one phone, all day, every day.** That single habit removes almost every London fare problem.

- **Tap in and out** on the Tube, Elizabeth line, Overground and National Rail. Buses are tap-in only.
- A **missed tap-out** charges a maximum fare — the most common overcharge visitors see.
- **Contactless equals Oyster** on fares and caps, so the £10 Oyster fee is usually wasted money.
- **Do not drive.** ULEZ covers effectively all of Greater London and the Congestion Charge applies in the centre; both are charged per day and enforced by camera.
- **Strikes** are announced in advance. Check before a travel day.

scams.body:
London is not a scam-heavy city. The recurring ones are:

- **The shell game** on Westminster Bridge and around Oxford Street — the same rigged three-cup game as Paris and Rome, with the same crowd of accomplices.
- **Unofficial ticket sellers** for shows and attractions around Leicester Square. The official half-price booth is a specific, signed building; the shops around it are not it.
- **Pickpocketing** on packed Tube carriages and in the West End at closing time.
- **Card machines handed over with a pre-set amount** in tourist-area bars — check the figure before you tap.

crowds.body:
London absorbs its visitors well; the crowding is specific rather than general. The pressure points are Oxford Street on Saturdays, the Tower and Westminster mid-morning, the major museums in school holidays, and the Tube at 08:00–09:30 and 17:00–18:30.

The free major museums genuinely are free and genuinely are excellent; they are also busiest between 11:00 and 15:00.

closures.body:
Two London-specific closure patterns:

- **Christmas Day.** The entire Tube network, most rail services and a very large share of restaurants and attractions close. There is no equivalent shutdown in most other European capitals, and it surprises visitors every year.
- **Engineering works and strikes.** Planned weekend closures on individual Tube lines are routine and posted in advance; strikes are announced days ahead.

neighborhoods.body:
London's neighbourhood risk for a visitor is mostly about convenience and noise rather than safety.

- **Around the main rail termini** (King's Cross, Victoria, Paddington) is convenient and less pleasant late at night than the price implies, though all have improved substantially.
- **The West End** is central and loud until late.
- **Zone 2 is a genuine saving** and rarely more than 15–20 minutes from the centre, provided you check the walk from the station.

Check the Tube line, not the map distance: "two miles from the centre" on the wrong line is a longer journey than four miles on the right one.

entry_requirements.body:
The UK now requires an **Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA)** in advance from many nationalities that previously needed nothing. This is the single most likely UK entry problem for a visitor who last came a few years ago.

Apply through the official UK government service only; a large number of lookalike sites charge a substantial markup for the same application. Check the current requirement for your nationality and your dates on the official government site well before you fly.

accommodation.body:
London hotel pricing is honest by international standards — the rate is broadly the rate, with VAT included in displayed prices. There is no widespread resort-fee culture.

The two things worth checking are room size (London rooms are small even at high prices, and "double" can mean genuinely tight) and whether the property is on a night-bus route or above a pub, both of which are noise questions the listing will not answer.

faqs.q: Should I buy an Oyster card or use contactless in London?
faqs.a: Contactless, for almost every visitor. Fares and the daily and weekly caps are identical to Oyster, you skip the £10 card fee, and there is no deposit to reclaim or leftover credit stranded when you fly home. The important part is using the same card or phone for every tap — switching between your phone and the physical card mid-day can stop journeys counting toward the same cap, even on the same bank account.

faqs.q: How much does London transport cost per day?
faqs.a: The Zones 1–2 daily cap is £8.90 and the Monday-to-Sunday cap for Zones 1–2 is £44.70. Once you hit the cap, further journeys that day are free. You must tap in and out on rail services — a missed tap-out triggers a maximum fare several times higher than the correct one.

faqs.q: Do I need to worry about ULEZ as a tourist?
faqs.a: Only if you drive. ULEZ now covers virtually all of Greater London within the M25, making it one of the world's largest low emission zones, and it is charged daily. The central Congestion Charge applies on top inside its zone. Both are camera-enforced. For a visitor the answer is almost always not to have a car in London at all.

destinations.risk_summary:
New York's trip-ruining problem is **cost density**, not danger. Hotel taxes total roughly **14.75%** — a $300 room carries about **$44.25** in percentage taxes plus flat per-night fees, including a city occupancy tax of 5.875% of room rent plus a flat nightly amount and a $1.50 state unit fee.

The other reliable money leak is location: the same burger that costs $20 in the East Village is $28–$32 in Times Square, and restaurants there charge 25–50% more than comparable places three blocks away.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes. New York is one of the few major cities where the practical advice is genuinely simple: use the subway, do not eat in Times Square, and book the one or two things that sell out.

The most common regret is a hotel chosen for its Times Square address, which buys noise, crowds and a premium on everything within walking distance.
destinations.worst_months: Late December (peak pricing), January–February (cold), July–August (heat and humidity)

overview.body:
New York is expensive in a straightforward way and safe in an ordinary big-city way. The mistakes that cost visitors most are locational — where you sleep and where you eat — rather than anything dramatic.

The subway is the single biggest saving available and the thing most first-time visitors underuse.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes. The city rewards walking and the subway, and punishes taxis in traffic and restaurants chosen by proximity to a landmark.

If you are choosing dates, April to early June and September to October give you the best weather. Late December is spectacular and the most expensive week of the year by a wide margin.

top_risks.body:
- **The hotel tax stack**, roughly **14.75%** in percentage taxes plus flat per-night fees.
- **Times Square pricing**, 25–50% above comparable places a few blocks away.
- **Taking taxis in traffic** when the subway is faster and a fraction of the cost.
- **Airport transfers**, which can exceed $70.
- **Broadway and major attraction tickets** bought from resellers at a markup.
- **Summer heat and humidity**, and January–February cold, both of which shorten walking days.

hidden_costs.body:
- **Hotel taxes total roughly 14.75%.** On a $300-a-night room that is about **$44.25** in percentage taxes, plus flat fees on top.
- The structure: a **city hotel room occupancy tax of 5.875%** of room rent plus a flat amount per night, and a **New York State unit fee of $1.50 per room per night**, alongside state and city sales taxes.
- **Resort/destination fees** have spread to a number of Manhattan hotels and are not in the compared rate.
- **Location premium.** Times Square and the areas immediately around major landmarks charge 25–50% more for the same quality — a $20 East Village burger is $28–$32 there, and a $1.50 bodega water is $3–$5.
- **Airport transfers** can run **$70 or more**; the subway is $3 a ride.

Mid-range visitors should budget roughly **$235–$385 per person per day**, assuming two sharing a room and mixing subway with occasional taxis.

neighborhoods.body:
**Why tourists regret staying near Times Square** is a fair question with a concrete answer.

It is not dangerous. It is loud around the clock, extremely crowded on the pavement, and — the part that actually costs money — everything within walking distance is priced for people who will not walk further. Restaurants charge 25–50% more than comparable places three blocks away; a bottle of water is $3–$5 against $1.50 at a neighbourhood deli.

The alternative is not far away. Midtown East, Chelsea, the Flatiron district, the Lower East Side and large parts of Brooklyn within 15 minutes on the subway are cheaper to sleep in and much cheaper to eat in. Given that the subway is $3 and runs all night, "central" buys you very little in New York.

transportation.body:
**The subway is the answer to most New York transport questions.** It is roughly $3 a ride, runs 24 hours, and beats a taxi on almost every Manhattan journey during the day.

- **Taxis are metered and include a 50-cent MTA tax**; the meter continues in traffic, which is the expensive part.
- **Airport transfers** can exceed $70 by car. AirTrain plus subway from JFK, and the subway or bus from LGA, are dramatically cheaper.
- **Check which airport your fare is for.** JFK, LaGuardia and Newark are in different states' worth of traffic from each other.
- Walking is genuinely competitive for anything under about 20 blocks.

scams.body:
New York's characteristic visitor problems are commercial rather than criminal.

- **Costumed characters in Times Square** who pose for a photo then demand payment, sometimes aggressively.
- **Ticket touts** for comedy clubs and bus tours who work Times Square on commission; the tour is real, the price is not.
- **Resold Broadway tickets** at a markup, or that do not exist. Buy from the theatre, TodayTix or the official TKTS booths.
- **Restaurants with no prices on the menu** near major landmarks.
- Ordinary **pickpocketing** on packed subway cars and in Times Square crowds.

crowds.body:
Crowding in New York is concentrated at Times Square, the observation decks, the 9/11 Memorial, the Statue of Liberty ferry and the major museums at weekends.

The observation decks and the Statue of Liberty ferry are the two things that genuinely require booking ahead. Everything else is manageable by going early or late.

weather.body:
New York has real seasons and both extremes shorten a walking-based trip.

- **July and August** are hot and very humid; the subway platforms are considerably hotter than the street.
- **January and February** are cold enough that outdoor plans need shortening and layering.
- **Late summer and autumn** carry a residual tropical-storm risk that occasionally disrupts flights.

April to early June and September to October are the comfortable windows.

entry_requirements.body:
International visitors need a US visa or, for eligible nationalities, an approved **ESTA** obtained in advance — not on arrival. Apply only through the official government site; lookalike sites charge a large markup for the identical application.

Check your own government's advice and official US guidance for your nationality and dates.

accommodation.body:
Two questions before you book:

1. **What is the all-in nightly total?** Roughly 14.75% in percentage taxes plus flat per-night fees, and increasingly a destination fee on top.
2. **Which subway lines are within a five-minute walk?** In New York this matters more than the neighbourhood name. A hotel two express stops from Midtown at a third of the Times Square premium is a better trip and a cheaper one.

faqs.q: How much tax is added to a New York hotel room?
faqs.a: Roughly 14.75% in percentage taxes, plus flat per-night fees. On a $300-a-night room that is about $44.25 in percentage taxes alone. The structure includes a city hotel room occupancy tax of 5.875% of room rent plus a flat nightly amount, and a New York State unit fee of $1.50 per room per night, alongside state and city sales taxes. A growing number of Manhattan hotels also add a destination or resort fee.

faqs.q: Why do tourists regret staying near Times Square?
faqs.a: Not because it is dangerous — because it is loud around the clock, extremely crowded on the pavement, and everything within walking distance is priced for people who will not walk further. Restaurants charge 25–50% more than comparable places three blocks away: a $20 East Village burger is $28–$32 there, and a $1.50 bodega water is $3–$5. With the subway at $3 and running 24 hours, a Times Square address buys very little.

faqs.q: Is the subway worth using in New York?
faqs.a: Yes — it is the single biggest saving available to a visitor. It costs roughly $3 a ride, runs 24 hours, and beats a taxi on most Manhattan journeys during the day because a taxi meter keeps running in traffic. Airport transfers by car can exceed $70; AirTrain plus subway from JFK costs a small fraction of that.

destinations.risk_summary:
Las Vegas has the most aggressive **fee structure of any major US destination**, and the advertised room rate is close to meaningless. Most major Strip hotels charge **$45–$55 a night in resort fees before tax**; the highest on the Strip as of April 2026 are **$62.36 a night** at Bellagio, The Cosmopolitan, Fontainebleau, The Venetian, The Palazzo and Vdara.

Parking is charged separately again — **$15–$35 self-park, $20–$45 valet** — and the 13.38% room tax applies to the resort fee as well as the room.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes, provided you price the trip on the all-in nightly figure rather than the headline rate. A $99 room with a $55 resort fee and $25 parking is a $179 room before tax, and Vegas is genuinely good value at $179 and poor value if you thought it was $99.

The year-to-date average daily rate for Strip hotels as of June 2026 is $208.02, with June alone averaging $165.45 — useful reference points for judging whether a deal is one.
destinations.worst_months: June–August (extreme heat), major convention weeks

overview.body:
Las Vegas is a destination where the pricing model is the main risk. Everything else — safety, transport, logistics — is straightforward.

The city has built an economy on the difference between an advertised rate and a final bill, and a visitor who understands that structure is fine. A visitor who does not is regularly out several hundred dollars over a long weekend.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes. Vegas delivers what it advertises; it just does not advertise the price.

Use the all-in number. As of June 2026 the year-to-date average daily rate on the Strip is $208.02 and June alone averaged $165.45 — if the all-in figure you are quoted is well below that, it is a genuine deal; if the headline rate is below it but the all-in is not, it is not.

top_risks.body:
- **Resort fees**, $45–$55 a night at most major Strip hotels and **$62.36** at the highest as of April 2026.
- **Parking charged separately**, $15–$35 self-park and $20–$45 valet.
- **13.38% room tax applied to the resort fee as well as the room.**
- **Extreme summer heat**, routinely over 40°C, which is a genuine health risk, not an inconvenience.
- **Convention weeks**, which multiply room rates without warning.
- **Taxi "long-hauling"** from the airport via the tunnel.

hidden_costs.body:
This is the defining risk of a Las Vegas trip.

- **Resort fees:** most major Strip hotels charge **$45–$55 per night before tax**. As of April 2026 the highest on the Strip are **$62.36 a night**, at Bellagio, The Cosmopolitan, Fontainebleau, The Venetian, The Palazzo and Vdara.
- **Room tax is 13.38%** (Clark County), and it is applied **to the resort fee as well as the room rate** — so a $55 resort fee is really about $62 out of pocket.
- **Parking is separate again:** most Strip hotels charge **$15–$35 a night for self-parking** and **$20–$45 for valet**. Treasure Island is the only major Strip hotel offering free self-parking to hotel guests.

A quoted $99 room is therefore commonly a $180+ night once resort fee, tax and parking are added. Price every Vegas comparison on the all-in figure or the comparison is meaningless.
