The ultimate guide to Vegas fees in 2026

weather.body:
Summer heat in Las Vegas is a safety issue rather than a comfort one. June to August routinely exceeds 40°C, and the Strip is a long, exposed walk between properties that look adjacent.

The distance between two casinos can be twenty minutes in direct sun. People are hospitalised for heat exhaustion here every summer, and the risk is highest for visitors who underestimate the walk because the buildings look close.

March to April and October to November are the comfortable windows.

transportation.body:
- **The Strip is much longer than it looks.** Adjacent-looking casinos are frequently a fifteen- to twenty-minute walk, much of it indoors through the properties.
- **Taxi long-hauling** from the airport — taking the tunnel and a longer route — is a known problem. Ask for the direct surface route, or use a rideshare with a quoted fare.
- **Parking is charged**, so a rental car is an additional nightly cost on top of the resort fee.
- The monorail and buses run the Strip; both are slower than they look on a map.

crowds.body:
Las Vegas crowding is convention-driven rather than seasonal. A large convention can triple room rates and fill every restaurant with no visible connection to the tourist calendar.

Before fixing dates, check the Las Vegas convention calendar for your week. It is the single most useful piece of Vegas trip planning and almost nobody does it.

scams.body:
Las Vegas's characteristic problems are commercial pressure rather than street crime.

- **Timeshare and vacation-club presentations** sold as free show tickets or discounted attractions. They cost a half-day and are high pressure.
- **Ticket resellers** on the Strip offering show tickets at a discount that is not one.
- **Taxi long-hauling** from the airport.
- **ATM fees** inside casinos, which are among the highest anywhere.

Street crime against visitors is not the main risk; the Strip is heavily surveilled and patrolled.

neighborhoods.body:
- **The Strip** is where most visitors stay and is where the fee structure is heaviest.
- **Downtown / Fremont Street** is cheaper, more compact, and has substantially lower resort fees — often the better value if you are not tied to a specific Strip property.
- **Off-Strip properties** avoid some fees but add a transport cost to everything.

The practical choice is between paying the Strip premium for walkability or saving downtown and accepting a rideshare each way.

entry_requirements.body:
International visitors need a US visa or, for eligible nationalities, an approved **ESTA** in advance. Apply only through the official government site; lookalike services charge a large markup for the identical application.

Check your own government's advice and official US guidance for your nationality and dates.

accommodation.body:
**Never compare Las Vegas hotels on the room rate.** The only meaningful number is room + resort fee + 13.38% tax on both + parking if you have a car.

Ask the property directly what the resort fee is and what it includes. If the answer is Wi-Fi, a gym and two bottles of water, that is a $50-a-night rate increase with a different name — and a hotel with a lower headline rate and a higher resort fee is frequently the more expensive stay.

faqs.q: How much are resort fees in Las Vegas in 2026?
faqs.a: Most major Strip hotels charge $45–$55 per night before tax. As of April 2026 the highest on the Strip are $62.36 a night, at Bellagio, The Cosmopolitan, Fontainebleau, The Venetian, The Palazzo and Vdara. The 13.38% Clark County room tax applies to the resort fee as well as the room, so a $55 fee is closer to $62 out of pocket.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay for parking in Las Vegas?
faqs.a: At almost every major Strip hotel, yes — typically $15–$35 a night for self-parking and $20–$45 for valet, charged separately from the resort fee. Treasure Island is the only major Strip hotel that still offers free self-parking to hotel guests.

faqs.q: What does a Las Vegas hotel room really cost?
faqs.a: Take the room rate, add the resort fee ($45–$62 a night on the Strip), add 13.38% tax on both, and add parking if you have a car. A quoted $99 room is commonly $180 or more per night in practice. For reference, the year-to-date average daily rate for Strip hotels as of June 2026 is $208.02, with June alone averaging $165.45.

destinations.risk_summary:
Cancún has three reliable trip-ruining problems: the **Visitax departure charge**, which hotels do not collect and which is enforced at the airport; **timeshare selling** that begins at the arrivals hall; and **sargassum seaweed**, which can make a beach you booked for unusable in season.

Visitax is **$15.80 per person** (283 pesos) for every foreign tourist departing Quintana Roo. The scam around it is that the top search results charge **$30–$40** for the same $15 tax.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes, with three specific pieces of homework: pay Visitax on the official site before you travel, decline everything offered between the baggage carousel and the exit, and check current sargassum reports for your dates and your specific stretch of coast.

Enforcement of Visitax was heightened in 2026, with checkpoints active at Terminals 3 and 4 — this is no longer something you can ignore.
destinations.worst_months: May–October (sargassum peak and hurricane season)

overview.body:
Cancún is an easy destination with a small number of specific, well-documented traps, all of which are avoidable with preparation and none of which are obvious on arrival.

The pattern is consistent: the problems begin at the airport, and they are commercial rather than criminal.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes. The resorts deliver, the sea is warm and the archaeology is genuinely worth the day trip.

What determines whether the trip works is the season. Sargassum can turn the beach you paid for into a clean-up operation, and it is highly seasonal and reasonably predictable — which means checking is worth more than hoping.

top_risks.body:
- **Visitax**, $15.80 per person, not collected by hotels, enforced at the airport, and widely resold at $30–$40 by lookalike sites.
- **Timeshare selling** from the moment you land.
- **Sargassum seaweed**, May to October, which can make a beach unusable.
- **Hurricane season**, June to November.
- **ATM and currency scams**, including dynamic currency conversion at a poor rate.
- **Unofficial airport transport** and taxi overcharging.

hidden_costs.body:
**Visitax is the one nobody warns you about.** It is a state tourism charge of **$15.80 USD per person (283 Mexican pesos)** payable by every foreign tourist departing Quintana Roo — which covers Cancún, Playa del Carmen, Tulum, Cozumel, Holbox, Isla Mujeres, Bacalar and the surrounding area.

Two things make it a trap:
1. **Hotels do not collect it**, and authorities have confirmed travellers must pay it separately. Many visitors assume it is bundled into the resort bill.
2. **The top search results for it are resellers charging $30–$40 for a $15 tax.** The official site is **visitax.gob.mx** and nothing else.

Enforcement was heightened in 2026, with checkpoints active at Terminals 3 and 4 — so an unpaid Visitax is now a problem at the airport rather than a theoretical one.

Other costs to expect: resort day-pass charges, tips (widely expected in USD), and dynamic currency conversion offered at card terminals at a poor rate — always choose to be charged in pesos.
sources: Cancún's $15.80 departure tax and airport enforcement
Travellers must pay Cancun Visitax separately — hotels won't collect it
Increased Visitax enforcement at Cancun airport for 2026

scams.body:
- **The Visitax markup.** Sites ranking above the official one charge $30–$40 for a $15.80 tax. Pay only at **visitax.gob.mx**.
- **Timeshare and vacation-club selling.** It starts in the arrivals hall, where people positioned near the exit present as transport or information staff. The offer is a free transfer, a discounted tour or a resort upgrade in exchange for a presentation. Decline everything until you are outside and at an official transport desk.
- **Dynamic currency conversion.** Card terminals offer to charge you in USD at a rate several per cent worse than your bank's. Always choose pesos.
- **ATM skimming** at standalone machines. Use bank-branded ATMs inside branches where possible.
- **Taxi overcharging.** Agree the fare before getting in; official rates are posted at the airport.
sources: The $40 Cancun scam targeting US tourists

weather.body:
Two separate seasonal problems, and they overlap.

**Sargassum.** Large volumes of seaweed wash ashore along the Caribbean coast, worst roughly **May to October**, and the state spends heavily on machinery and clean-up crews to keep beaches swimmable — the Visitax revenue is explicitly used partly for this. Sargassum varies enormously by beach and by week. Check current reports for your specific stretch of coast close to your dates; a resort's own photography will not show it.

**Hurricane season** runs **June to November**, peaking August to October. Direct hits are not common in a given year but disruption is a realistic possibility, and travel insurance covering weather disruption is worth considerably more in that window.

transportation.body:
- **Book airport transfers in advance** with a named operator, or use the official transport desks inside the terminal. Anyone approaching you before you reach those desks is selling something else.
- **ADO buses** between Cancún, Playa del Carmen and Tulum are comfortable, cheap and reliable.
- **Rental cars** are fine on the highway; be aware of insurance requirements, which are mandatory in Mexico and frequently the source of a large upcharge at the desk. Confirm what your booking includes in writing.
- **Colectivos** are the cheap local option along the coast.

crowds.body: Peak season is December to April, with spring break in March adding a distinct crowd to the hotel zone. Chichén Itzá is busiest between 11:00 and 14:00 when the tour buses from Cancún arrive — going early is the difference between a good visit and a queue.

neighborhoods.body:
- **The Hotel Zone** is the strip of resorts on the barrier island: convenient, insulated, and where the beach-quality question actually matters.
- **Downtown Cancún** is cheaper, real, and not a beach location.
- **Playa del Carmen and Tulum** are separate trips with separate characters; Tulum in particular is considerably more expensive than its reputation suggests.

If beach quality is the point of your trip, research the specific stretch rather than the resort brand — sargassum does not respect star ratings.

entry_requirements.body:
Mexico's entry requirements depend on nationality; many visitors receive a tourist permit on arrival. Check your own government's advice for your dates.

The charge that catches people out is not entry but exit: **Visitax**, $15.80 per person, payable by every foreign tourist departing Quintana Roo, not collected by hotels, and enforced at airport checkpoints. Pay it at visitax.gob.mx before you travel.

accommodation.body:
Confirm two things before booking:

1. **What the all-inclusive actually includes** — premium spirits, à-la-carte restaurants, motorised watersports and off-site excursions are frequently extra.
2. **The beach situation for your dates.** Ask the property directly about sargassum for the season you are visiting and what their clean-up arrangement is. A property that answers specifically is telling you something; one that answers with photographs is telling you something else.

faqs.q: What is Visitax and do I have to pay it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are a foreign tourist departing Quintana Roo — which covers Cancún, Playa del Carmen, Tulum, Cozumel, Holbox, Isla Mujeres and Bacalar. It is $15.80 USD per person (283 Mexican pesos). Hotels do not collect it, so many visitors assume wrongly that it is on the resort bill. Enforcement was heightened in 2026 with checkpoints at Terminals 3 and 4.

faqs.q: How do I avoid the Visitax scam?
faqs.a: Pay only at the official site, visitax.gob.mx. The problem is that sites ranking above the official one in search results charge $30–$40 for the same $15.80 tax. There is no service being provided for the difference.

faqs.q: When is sargassum seaweed worst in Cancun?
faqs.a: Roughly May to October. It varies enormously by beach and by week, and the state spends heavily on machinery and clean-up crews — some of the Visitax revenue is explicitly used for this. Check current sargassum reports for your specific stretch of coast close to your dates; a resort's own marketing photography will not show it.

destinations.risk_summary:
Tokyo is one of the safest and best-run cities a visitor can go to, and almost every problem here is **logistical and recently changed**. Three 2026 changes matter: the departure tax **tripled from ¥1,000 to ¥3,000** in July 2026, the tourist-facing Pasmo Passport IC card was **discontinued in 2024** (so most guides still recommend a card you cannot buy), and climbing Mount Fuji now carries a **mandatory ¥4,000 fee** on every official trail.

Cash also still matters more than visitors expect.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes, without qualification. The risk here is being caught out by an out-of-date guide rather than by anything about the city.

Check the IC card situation before you land, budget the higher departure tax, and carry more cash than feels necessary.
destinations.best_months: March–April (cherry blossom, book far ahead), October–November
destinations.worst_months: June–August (heat and humidity), Golden Week, Obon, New Year

overview.body:
Tokyo's risk profile is unusual: crime against visitors is very low, the transport is excellent, and the food is safe. What ruins trips here is friction — a payment method that does not work, a reservation system nobody told you about, or a national holiday week that fills every train.

Almost all of it is solved by preparation rather than caution.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes. The honest caveats are seasonal and financial rather than about the city: cherry-blossom season needs booking many months ahead, summer is genuinely oppressive, and the yen's movement has made Japan cheaper for some visitors and not others.

Golden Week, Obon and New Year are domestic travel peaks — trains and hotels fill with Japanese travellers, not tourists, and availability collapses.

top_risks.body:
- **The departure tax tripled to ¥3,000** in July 2026, included in your ticket.
- **The Pasmo Passport was discontinued in 2024** — most guides still recommend it.
- **Mount Fuji now charges ¥4,000** per climber on every official trail.
- **Cash.** Smaller ryokan and traditional inns often take cash only, including for accommodation tax.
- **Domestic holiday peaks** (Golden Week, Obon, New Year) which fill trains and hotels.
- **Summer heat and humidity**, which are severe.

hidden_costs.body:
- **Departure tax: ¥3,000 per person from July 2026**, tripled from ¥1,000. It applies to everyone leaving Japan, foreign visitors and Japanese citizens alike, and is included directly in your air or ferry ticket — so it is not a queue at the airport, but it is a real price increase.
- **Mount Fuji: ¥4,000 mandatory hiking fee** per climber on every official route. Climbing is no longer free on any trail.
- **Accommodation tax** is levied by several municipalities including Tokyo, and smaller properties frequently require it in cash.
- **IC card deposits and top-ups** — see transport.

Japan is not a fee-heavy destination by European or US standards; the issue is that several of these charges are new enough that older guidance misses them.
sources: Japan tourist tax 2026: departure tax now ¥3,000
Japan tourist rules 2026: new fees and fines

transportation.body:
**The IC card situation is the single most changed piece of Japan travel logistics, and most guides are wrong about it.**

The **Pasmo Passport** — the tourist-facing IC card that a large share of published guidance still recommends — was **discontinued in 2024**. If you arrive planning to buy one, you cannot.

The working alternatives are **phone-based Suica or PASMO** in Apple Wallet or Google Wallet, set up before you travel. This is the smoothest option and avoids the physical-card supply problem entirely.

Beyond that, Tokyo's transport is exceptional and cheap. The main visitor mistakes are underestimating interchange walking distances at the largest stations (Shinjuku and Tokyo station are small towns) and assuming the last train is later than it is — most lines stop around midnight.
sources: Japan travel tips for 2026: what actually matters on the ground

crowds.body:
Tokyo's crowd peaks are domestic, which is why they surprise foreign visitors.

- **Golden Week** (late April to early May), **Obon** (mid-August) and **New Year** are the periods when the whole country travels. Trains and hotels fill, prices rise and availability collapses.
- **Cherry-blossom season** (late March to early April) is the international peak and requires booking many months ahead.

Outside those, Tokyo absorbs visitors remarkably well for a city of its size.

weather.body:
- **June to August** is hot and extremely humid, with heat that makes long walking days genuinely difficult. This is under-communicated in most guidance.
- **The rainy season** runs roughly June to mid-July.
- **Typhoon season** peaks August to October and can disrupt flights and rail.
- **March–April and October–November** are the comfortable windows.

scams.body:
Tokyo has very little in the way of tourist scams by international standards. The recurring exception is **touting in Kabukicho and Roppongi** — people offering to take you to a bar, where the bill is enormous and payment is pressured. Do not follow a tout to any venue.

Otherwise, the practical risks are administrative rather than criminal: a card that will not work, a restaurant that takes cash only, a reservation system that requires a Japanese phone number.

neighborhoods.body:
Tokyo's neighbourhood question is about convenience, not safety.

- **Shinjuku and Shibuya** are the most connected and the loudest.
- **Around Tokyo station and Ginza** is quieter and suits a Shinkansen-based itinerary.
- **Asakusa and the east** is cheaper and more traditional, with a longer commute to the west-side nightlife.

The real check is which line the nearest station is on and how many changes that means to the places you actually plan to go — an address that looks central on a map can be three changes from everything.

entry_requirements.body:
Japan's entry requirements depend on nationality and have been changing. Check the official Japanese government guidance and your own government's travel advice for your dates.

Japan has also been introducing pre-travel electronic systems; confirm what is required for your nationality well before departure rather than assuming visa-free entry on the basis of an older trip.

accommodation.body:
Two Japan-specific checks:

- **Room size.** Standard Tokyo hotel rooms are small by international standards, and the listed square metres are accurate. If space matters, filter on it explicitly.
- **Payment method.** Larger hotels take cards; smaller ryokan and traditional inns frequently do not, and may require cash for the accommodation tax even when they take cards for the room. Carry a few thousand yen for this.

faqs.q: How much is Japan's departure tax in 2026?
faqs.a: ¥3,000 per person, tripled from ¥1,000 in July 2026. It applies to everyone leaving Japan — foreign visitors and Japanese citizens alike — and is included directly in your airline or ferry ticket, so there is no separate queue to pay it.

faqs.q: Can I still buy a Pasmo Passport in Japan?
faqs.a: No. The Pasmo Passport — the tourist-facing IC card that a large amount of published guidance still recommends — was discontinued in 2024. Use a phone-based Suica or PASMO set up in Apple Wallet or Google Wallet before you travel; that avoids the physical-card supply problem entirely.

faqs.q: Is it still free to climb Mount Fuji?
faqs.a: No. Since 2025 every climber on every official trail pays a mandatory ¥4,000 hiking fee. There is no longer a free official route.

faqs.q: Do I need cash in Tokyo?
faqs.a: More than you would expect. Larger hotels, chains and major attractions take cards, but smaller ryokan, traditional inns and many small restaurants are cash-only, and some properties require the accommodation tax in cash even when they accept cards for the room. Carry a few thousand yen.

destinations.risk_summary:
Bangkok's problems are **commercial and atmospheric**. The defining scam is the "**the Grand Palace is closed today**" approach, which funnels visitors into tuk-tuk gem and tailor commission tours — the palace is in fact open every day, 08:30 to 15:30, and entry is ฿500 at the gate.

The other reliable one is the taxi that will not use the meter: a metered airport run to central Bangkok is roughly **500–600 THB plus a 50 THB expressway toll**, against the **1,200–1,500 THB** flat fare commonly quoted.

Air quality in the dry months is a genuine health consideration.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes. Bangkok is not dangerous for visitors in any ordinary sense; it is a city where a small number of well-rehearsed commercial approaches account for most bad experiences, and all of them are defeated by knowing the two facts above.

If you have a respiratory condition, check air quality data for your dates before committing to the dry season.
destinations.best_months: November–February (cool, dry — but check air quality)
destinations.worst_months: March–May (extreme heat), and dry-season smog peaks

overview.body:
Bangkok is a large, hot, chaotic and generally very safe city where the risks to a visitor are almost entirely commercial: a driver who will not use the meter, a stranger who redirects your day, a tour that turns out to be a shopping trip.

The city is also genuinely enjoyable once you stop being a target for those, which mostly means knowing two or three specific facts.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes. The temples, the food and the river are worth the trip on their own.

The two things to plan around are heat — March to May is punishing — and air quality, which in the dry months can be poor enough to matter for anyone with a respiratory condition.

top_risks.body:
- **The "Grand Palace is closed" scam**, which redirects your day into a commission shopping tour.
- **Taxis refusing the meter**, especially at the airport and outside hotels.
- **PM2.5 air pollution** during the dry months.
- **Heat**, particularly March to May.
- **Tuk-tuk "tour" offers** at implausibly low prices, which are commission runs.
- **Dress code enforcement** at the Grand Palace and major temples — shoulders and knees covered.

scams.body:
**"The Grand Palace is closed today."** This is the defining Bangkok scam and it is well organised. Someone official-looking near the entrance — sometimes in something resembling a uniform — tells you the palace is closed for a ceremony, a holiday or a private event, and helpfully arranges a tuk-tuk to take you elsewhere. The elsewhere is a gem shop and a tailor, both paying commission, and the day is gone.

**The Grand Palace is open every day, 08:30 to 15:30.** Entry is **฿500 per person**, purchased at the gate — there is no online booking on the official site. Children under 120cm are free; above that they pay the adult ฿500 regardless of age.

**Taxis refusing the meter.** Drivers near hotels and tourist sites frequently decline the meter and quote a flat fare. From Suvarnabhumi Airport to central Bangkok the quoted flat fare is commonly **1,200–1,500 THB**; the metered fare is roughly **500–600 THB plus a 50 THB expressway toll**. Insist on the meter, or walk to the next taxi — there is always a next taxi.

**The tuk-tuk day tour at an impossible price.** A 20-baht all-day tour is a series of commission stops.

**Gem and tailor shops** reached via any of the above. There is no wholesale gem opportunity for tourists.
sources: Grand Palace Bangkok 2026: tickets, hours and dress code
Bangkok travel safety: tuk-tuk scams and money protection (2026)

hidden_costs.body:
- **Grand Palace: ฿500 per person**, gate purchase only. Children under 120cm free; over that height it is the full ฿500 regardless of age, which surprises families.
- **Dual pricing** is normal at some attractions — a foreign-visitor rate distinct from the local rate. It is posted and legal.
- **Airport taxi**: metered 500–600 THB plus a 50 THB expressway toll, versus 1,200–1,500 THB commonly quoted as a flat fare.
- **Temple dress**: shops outside the major temples sell cover-ups at tourist prices to people who arrive in shorts. Bring your own.
sources: Grand Palace Bangkok: complete visitor's guide 2026

transportation.body:
- **Insist on the meter.** If the driver refuses, get out. This is the single most useful habit in Bangkok.
- **Grab (the ride app) removes the negotiation entirely** and is widely used.
- **The BTS Skytrain and MRT** are fast, cheap, air-conditioned and avoid the traffic, which is severe. Where they go, use them.
- **River boats** are a genuine transport option for the temple district, not just a tourist experience.
- **Traffic** is bad enough that a 6km taxi journey at the wrong hour can take an hour.

health_safety.body:
**Air quality is the underrated Bangkok risk.** During the dry months Bangkok and northern Thailand can experience hazardous smog, with PM2.5 reaching levels that matter for children, older travellers and anyone with a respiratory condition.

Monitor the AQI for your dates and limit outdoor activity when values peak. This is not a theoretical concern — it regularly reaches levels at which authorities advise limiting outdoor exertion.

Beyond air: tap water is not for drinking, street food is generally safe at busy stalls with high turnover, and travel insurance with medical cover is worth having given the quality and cost of private hospitals.

weather.body:
- **March to May is the hot season** and is genuinely extreme — walking temple itineraries in that window is difficult.
- **June to October is the rainy season**, with heavy but usually short afternoon downpours and occasional flooding.
- **November to February is the cool, dry season** and the best time to visit, with the caveat that it overlaps the worst air-quality months.

There is no month that is simultaneously cool, dry and clear-aired; pick which trade you prefer.

crowds.body:
Bangkok is busy but absorbs visitors well. The pressure points are the Grand Palace between 09:00 and 11:00, Wat Pho and Wat Arun mid-morning, and the weekend markets.

Going to the Grand Palace at opening (08:30) is a materially different experience from arriving at 10:00.

neighborhoods.body:
- **Sukhumvit** is well connected by BTS, full of hotels, and varies sharply block by block — some sois are family-friendly and some are the nightlife district.
- **Silom / Sathorn** is the business district, well connected and quieter at night.
- **Riverside** is the most pleasant and the least connected to the metro.
- **Khao San Road** is the backpacker centre and is loud until very late.

Check the specific soi number, not just the road name — that is where the variation is.

entry_requirements.body:
Thailand's entry requirements depend on nationality and have changed repeatedly, including the introduction of electronic arrival systems. Check the official Thai government guidance and your own government's advice for your dates rather than relying on an older trip's experience.

Proof of onward travel is requested more consistently in Thailand than in many destinations.

accommodation.body:
Check the distance to the nearest BTS or MRT station in walking minutes, not kilometres — Bangkok's heat and pavements make a 1.2km walk a different proposition from the same distance elsewhere.

For the same reason, a hotel on the wrong side of a major road can be a fifteen-minute detour to the nearest crossing.

faqs.q: Is the Grand Palace ever closed?
faqs.a: It is open every day from 08:30 to 15:30. Anyone telling you it is closed for a ceremony, holiday or private event is running the best-known scam in Bangkok — the next step is a tuk-tuk to a gem shop and a tailor, both paying commission. Entry is ฿500 per person, bought at the gate; there is no online booking on the official site.

faqs.q: How much should a taxi from Bangkok airport cost?
faqs.a: On the meter, roughly 500–600 THB to central Bangkok plus a 50 THB expressway toll. Drivers commonly quote a flat 1,200–1,500 THB instead. Insist on the meter or take the next taxi; alternatively use Grab, which quotes the fare up front and removes the negotiation.

faqs.q: Is air pollution a problem in Bangkok?
faqs.a: During the dry months, yes. Bangkok and northern Thailand can experience hazardous smog with PM2.5 at levels that matter for children, older travellers and anyone with a respiratory condition. Monitor the AQI for your dates and limit outdoor activity when values peak — the cool dry season that is otherwise the best time to visit overlaps the worst air-quality window.

destinations.risk_summary:
Istanbul's problems are **pricing and payment**, and they are concentrated at exactly the places a first-time visitor goes. Hagia Sophia now charges foreign visitors **€25** for the visiting area. The Blue Mosque is **free**, which does not stop unofficial sellers bundling it into paid "Hagia Sophia & Blue Mosque entry" packages.

The payment scam to know is the **calculator/terminal trick**: a cashier shows one price and charges a higher amount on the card terminal. Always read the terminal before you tap.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes, emphatically. Istanbul rewards a visitor who buys tickets through official channels and reads card terminals, and punishes one who does neither.

The practical baseline: get an IstanbulKart on arrival, buy museum tickets through the official Müze app, and use a metered or app-based taxi with the expectation that tolls are added on top.
destinations.worst_months: July–August (heat and crowds), January–February (cold and wet)

overview.body:
Istanbul is a very large, very rewarding city where the visitor risk is commercial rather than criminal. The specific approaches are well documented and repeat in the same few squares.

The city is also excellent value on public transport and food, which makes the contrast with the tourist-facing pricing sharper than it needs to be.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes. Very few cities offer this much at this price once you are past the tourist-facing layer.

April–May and September–October give you comfortable temperatures and manageable queues at the major sites.

top_risks.body:
- **The card-terminal trick** — a different amount charged than the one you were shown.
- **Unofficial ticket bundling**, especially packages including the free Blue Mosque.
- **Airport taxi overcharging**, and tolls added on top of the meter.
- **Single-ticket transport pricing**, 2–3× the IstanbulKart fare.
- **The shoeshine and restaurant-tout approaches** around Sultanahmet.
- **Summer heat** in a city with substantial walking between sights.

scams.body:
- **The calculator / card-terminal trick.** The cashier shows one price on a calculator or verbally, then presents a terminal with a higher amount. **Read the terminal screen before you tap or enter a PIN**, every time. This is the most costly and most common Istanbul scam.
- **Bundled "entry" packages.** Unofficial vendors sell "Hagia Sophia & Blue Mosque entry" — but **the Blue Mosque is free to enter**. You are paying for something that costs nothing. Book Hagia Sophia and Topkapı in advance through the **official Müze app**.
- **Airport taxis.** Toll roads are commonly used on airport routes and the tolls are added on top of the meter, which is legitimate but is also cover for inflated totals. Use an app-based ride or an official rank, and expect the toll line.
- **The dropped shoeshine brush.** A shoeshine man drops a brush, you helpfully return it, and you are then given an unwanted shine and asked for a large sum.
- **The restaurant tout / bar setup.** A friendly stranger suggests a bar; the bill is enormous and payment is pressured. Do not follow strangers to venues.
sources: Is Istanbul safe for tourists? 8 scams to avoid (2026)

hidden_costs.body:
- **Hagia Sophia: €25 for foreign visitors** for the guided visiting area (upper gallery and museum zones). Both euros and lira are accepted at the counter, with euros recommended.
- **The Blue Mosque is free.** Any package charging for it is charging for nothing.
- **Transport:** a tram, metro or bus ride is about **42 TL (≈€1)** on an IstanbulKart. **Single tickets cost 2–3× as much** — getting a card on arrival is the single easiest saving in the city.
- **Airport taxi tolls** are added on top of the metered fare.
- **Bazaar pricing** is negotiable by design; the first price is not the price.
sources: How much does Istanbul cost in 2026?

transportation.body:
**Get an IstanbulKart at the airport or the first station you use.** It works on the metro, tram, Marmaray, ferries and buses, and single tickets cost two to three times as much.

- **A ride is roughly 42 TL (about €1)** on the card.
- **The ferries are public transport**, not a tour, and are the best way to cross the Bosphorus.
- **Taxis:** use an app or an official rank, insist on the meter, and expect tolls to be added on airport routes. The combination of a legitimate toll and an illegitimate markup is where visitors lose money.
sources: Istanbul taxi guide 2026: fares, apps and scam tips

crowds.body:
Sultanahmet — Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque, Topkapı and the Basilica Cistern within a few hundred metres — absorbs the overwhelming majority of visitors, and mid-morning in summer is the peak.

Going at opening, or late in the afternoon, materially changes the experience. The rest of the city is far less pressured.

weather.body:
- **July and August** are hot and humid, and Istanbul involves substantial walking on hills between sights.
- **January and February** are cold, grey and wet, with occasional snow.
- **April–May and September–October** are the comfortable windows and also the best light for the city.

neighborhoods.body:
- **Sultanahmet** puts you next to the major sights and is the most tourist-facing part of the city, with the pricing and touting that implies.
- **Beyoğlu / Galata / Karaköy** is where the city actually eats and drinks, and is a tram ride from the sights.
- **Kadıköy**, on the Asian side, is excellent value and a ferry ride away — a genuinely different and often better trip.

Check the hill. Istanbul's topography turns a 400m walk into a serious climb in several neighbourhoods.

entry_requirements.body:
Türkiye requires an **e-Visa** in advance from many nationalities. Apply only through the official government e-Visa site — there is a large ecosystem of lookalike sites charging several times the official fee for the identical document.

Check your own government's advice and the official Turkish e-Visa site for your nationality and dates.

accommodation.body:
Confirm the currency your rate is quoted in and what the property will actually charge — Istanbul rates are variously advertised in lira, euros and dollars, and the conversion is where the difference appears.

Also check what "walking distance to Hagia Sophia" means in practice: in Sultanahmet it is usually true; elsewhere it can mean a steep 25-minute climb.

faqs.q: How much does Hagia Sophia cost in 2026?
faqs.a: Foreign visitors pay €25 for the guided visiting area (the upper gallery and museum zones). Both euros and Turkish lira are accepted at the counter, with euros recommended. Book through the official Müze app rather than a third-party reseller.

faqs.q: Is the Blue Mosque free to enter?
faqs.a: Yes. That is why unofficial vendors bundle it into packages titled things like "Hagia Sophia & Blue Mosque Entry" — you are being charged for something that costs nothing. Buy Hagia Sophia and Topkapı tickets through the official Müze app and walk into the Blue Mosque for free.

faqs.q: What is the calculator scam in Istanbul?
faqs.a: A cashier shows you one price — on a calculator, or verbally — and then presents a card terminal with a higher amount. It works because people tap or enter a PIN without reading the screen. The defence is simple and complete: read the amount on the terminal before you authorise it, every single time.

faqs.q: Do I need an IstanbulKart?
faqs.a: It is the easiest saving in the city. A tram, metro or bus ride is about 42 TL (roughly €1) on the card, and single tickets cost two to three times as much. One card covers the metro, tram, Marmaray, ferries and buses.

destinations.risk_summary:
Dubai is safe, orderly and expensive, and the risks are **legal and climatic rather than criminal**. The Tourism Dirham fee is **AED 7–20 per room per night** (per room, not per person, capped at 30 consecutive nights), with a **7% municipality fee** and **5% VAT** on top.

Alcohol is legal in licensed venues and hotel rooms but public intoxication, open containers in public and drinking outside licensed premises remain illegal — and Dubai reinstated its **30% municipal tax on alcohol** on 1 January 2025, which is why the bar bill is what it is.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes, if you go in the right months and understand the rules. Summer heat in Dubai is not a discomfort, it is a constraint on what is possible outdoors.

The legal environment is the other thing to take seriously: the rules are clear, consistently enforced, and unforgiving of the assumption that tourist status is a defence.
destinations.worst_months: June–September (extreme heat)

overview.body:
Dubai is one of the lowest-crime destinations a visitor can choose, and the things that go wrong here are of a different type entirely: heat that limits the day, charges that are layered onto a room rate, and laws whose enforcement does not soften for tourists.

None of this makes it a difficult destination. It makes it one where reading the rules in advance actually matters.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes, in the cooler months. Between June and September the outdoor city is effectively unusable in the middle of the day and the trip becomes a sequence of air-conditioned interiors — which some people enjoy and most did not budget for.

November to March is when Dubai delivers what it advertises.

top_risks.body:
- **Extreme summer heat**, June to September.
- **The room-charge stack**: Tourism Dirham fee plus 7% municipality fee plus 5% VAT.
- **Alcohol rules** — licensed venues and private accommodation only; public intoxication and open containers are illegal.
- **Public-behaviour laws** that are enforced consistently regardless of visitor status.
- **Resort and beach-club charges**, which are substantial.
- **Salik road tolls**, charged electronically and billed through rental companies.

hidden_costs.body:
Dubai's accommodation charging is layered but stable — the Department of Economy and Tourism has confirmed the Tourism Dirham fee is unchanged for 2025/2026.

- **Tourism Dirham fee: AED 7–20 per room per night**, depending on the property's classification. It is charged **per room, not per person**, and is **capped at 30 consecutive nights**.
- **Municipality fee: 7%** of the booking total.
- **VAT: 5%**, included in the price.
- **Alcohol** carries a **30% municipal tax**, reinstated on 1 January 2025 after a two-year suspension — a material increase in bar and restaurant bills.
- **Salik road tolls** are charged electronically and billed through rental companies with an administration fee.

Consultants expect the 2026 tourism regulatory changes to bring more standardised disclosure of resort charges and clearer price displays across booking channels — which is an acknowledgement that current disclosure is inconsistent.
sources: Dubai Tourism Dirham fee — official rates 2026
Dubai tourist tax 2026: rates, rules and examples
Can you drink alcohol in Dubai? Complete 2026 rules

health_safety.body:
**Heat is the main physical risk.** From June to September, daytime temperatures make sustained outdoor activity genuinely dangerous, not merely uncomfortable. The government has run shortened summer working hours since 2024 in response.

Practically: plan outdoor activity for early morning or after sunset in those months, carry water, and treat the walk between two air-conditioned buildings as a real exposure.

Crime against visitors is very low. Medical care is excellent and expensive — travel insurance is worth having.

entry_requirements.body:
UAE entry requirements vary considerably by nationality — some receive a visa on arrival, others must apply in advance. Check the official UAE government guidance and your own government's travel advice for your dates.

Also worth checking before you fly: **medication rules**. The UAE restricts a number of medicines that are available over the counter elsewhere, including some codeine-based painkillers and some prescription drugs. Carrying a restricted medication without documentation is a serious matter, not a formality.

scams.body:
Dubai has very little street scamming by international standards. The recurring commercial issues are **unlicensed tour and desert-safari operators**, **timeshare and holiday-club presentations**, and **taxi drivers taking longer routes**.

Book activities with licensed operators, use metered taxis or ride apps, and be aware that any offer requiring you to attend a presentation costs you a half-day.

weather.body:
Dubai's weather is the single biggest determinant of whether the trip works.

- **June to September:** extreme heat and high humidity. Outdoor activity in the middle of the day is not realistic. Beaches, pools and outdoor attractions become early-morning and evening propositions.
- **November to March:** genuinely pleasant, warm and dry. This is the season the city is designed around, and prices reflect it.
- **April–May and October** are transitional and can go either way.

Booking a summer trip on a shoulder-season price is the most common Dubai mistake.

crowds.body:
Dubai handles volume well and general crowding is not a problem. The pressure points are the Burj Khalifa observation decks — which need booking ahead for sunset slots specifically — and the malls at weekends.

Note that the local weekend is Saturday–Sunday, with Friday prayers affecting some opening hours.

neighborhoods.body:
- **Dubai Marina and JBR** are walkable by Dubai standards and beach-adjacent.
- **Downtown** puts you at the Burj Khalifa and the mall, and is the most expensive.
- **Deira and Bur Dubai** are the older city, much cheaper, and a longer trip to the beaches.
- **Palm Jumeirah** is resort territory and requires a car or taxi for everything.

Dubai is not a walking city outside a few districts; check what is reachable on foot in the heat rather than on the map.

accommodation.body:
Ask for the all-in nightly total: room, Tourism Dirham fee (AED 7–20 per room per night), 7% municipality fee and 5% VAT.

Then check whether beach and pool access at your property is included or charged — beach-club day rates in Dubai are substantial, and "beach access" in a listing does not always mean free.

faqs.q: How much is Dubai's tourist tax?
faqs.a: The Tourism Dirham fee is AED 7–20 per room per night depending on the property's classification, charged per room rather than per person and capped at 30 consecutive nights. On top of that a 7% municipality fee applies to the booking total, and 5% VAT is included in the price. The Department of Economy and Tourism has confirmed the fee is unchanged for 2025/2026.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol in Dubai as a tourist?
faqs.a: Yes, in licensed venues and in hotel rooms or private rental accommodation. Alcohol may only be served at establishments holding a valid licence. Public intoxication, transporting open containers and drinking outside licensed premises remain illegal and are enforced. Dubai also reinstated a 30% municipal tax on alcohol sales on 1 January 2025 after a two-year suspension, which noticeably increased prices.

faqs.q: How bad is the summer heat in Dubai?
faqs.a: Severe enough to be a constraint rather than a discomfort. Between June and September, sustained outdoor activity in the middle of the day is not realistic, and the government has run shortened summer working hours since 2024 in response. Plan outdoor activity for early morning or after sunset, or travel between November and March.

destinations.risk_summary:
Mexico City's two most underrated risks are **physiological, not criminal**: it sits at **2,240 metres**, high enough that arrivals from sea level regularly lose their first day to altitude symptoms, and its air quality frequently exceeds WHO guidelines, particularly during thermal inversions.

The crime picture is more ordinary than its reputation: petty theft dominates the statistics affecting tourists, concentrated on the Metro. The airport taxi rank is where visitors most often get overcharged — and as of 2026 Uber pickup at the airport is restricted to specific pedestrian-bridge zones signed 'App Ride Pickup', not the kerb.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes, and it is badly undersold by its reputation. The central neighbourhoods most visitors use — Roma, Condesa, Polanco, Coyoacán, Centro Histórico, San Ángel — are broadly considered safe for daytime tourism.

What actually costs people a day is the altitude. Plan the first day light. Almost nobody does, and a meaningful share of visitors spend it with a headache instead.
destinations.worst_months: June–September (rainy season), winter thermal-inversion smog peaks

overview.body:
Mexico City is a very large, very rewarding capital where the risks a visitor actually meets are different from the ones the reputation predicts. Altitude, air quality and taxi overcharging account for far more ruined days than anything violent.

The practical version: arrive gently, use apps rather than street taxis, and keep valuables out of sight on the Metro.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes. The food, the museums and the neighbourhoods are as good as anywhere in the Americas, and the city is far cheaper than its peers.

The honest caveats are the first-day altitude adjustment and the seasonal air quality — neither is a reason not to go, both are reasons to plan the shape of the trip.

top_risks.body:
- **Altitude.** 2,240 metres. Headache, fatigue, breathlessness and disrupted sleep are normal on day one.
- **Air quality**, frequently above WHO guidelines and worst during thermal inversions.
- **Airport taxi overcharging**, and the 2026 change to where Uber can collect you.
- **Pickpocketing on the Metro**, particularly the airport-connecting lines.
- **Tap water** — not for drinking, and ice outside reputable venues is a risk.
- **Rainy-season afternoons**, June to September.

health_safety.body:
**Altitude is the risk nobody plans for.** Mexico City sits at **2,240 metres**, and the drop in available oxygen from sea level is noticeable. Symptoms include headache, fatigue, shortness of breath and disrupted sleep. Most people acclimatise within **24 to 48 hours** by staying hydrated, avoiding alcohol on the first day, and not scheduling anything strenuous.

Book the first day light. A visitor who lands and immediately does a full walking itinerary plus a big first night out reliably loses day two.

**Air quality** is a persistent concern: the metropolitan area frequently exceeds WHO pollution guidelines, particularly during thermal inversions that trap pollutants over the valley. On high-pollution days, anyone with a respiratory condition should limit outdoor exertion and consider an N95 mask — readily available at any farmacia.

**Water:** drink sealed bottled water and avoid ice outside reputable venues.

**Crime:** petty theft dominates the statistics affecting tourists, with pickpocketing frequent on the Metro, particularly the lines serving the airport and popular destinations. Use ATMs inside banks or hotels, and keep a backup card separate from your wallet.
sources: Is Mexico City safe? Travel risks and planning 2026
The tourist's guide to safety in Mexico City — Travel Guard

transportation.body:
**A 2026 change worth knowing before you land:** Uber pickup at Mexico City airport is restricted to specific pedestrian-bridge zones. Follow the signs for **'App Ride Pickup'** rather than expecting a kerbside collection — visitors who wait at the kerb wait a long time.

- **Street taxis at the airport and bus stations** frequently do not use meters, quote inflated prices, or have rigged meters. Taxi touts in the arrivals area quote inflated fares as a matter of course.
- **Use the authorised taxi stands inside the terminal**, hotel-arranged transport, or Uber/DiDi.
- **The Metro is cheap, fast and where the pickpocketing is.** It is fine to use; keep nothing in a back pocket and nothing loose in an open bag, especially on the airport-connecting lines.
- **Traffic** is severe; budget generously for any timed commitment.

scams.body:
- **Airport taxi touting.** People in the arrivals area presenting as transport staff, quoting several times the real fare. Walk past them to the official stands inside the terminal.
- **Rigged meters** in street taxis. If the meter climbs implausibly fast, ask to stop and pay what is fair.
- **ATM skimming** at standalone machines. Use machines inside bank branches or hotels.
- **Dynamic currency conversion** at card terminals — always choose to be charged in pesos, not your home currency.
- **Distraction theft on the Metro** at the doors as they close, the same pattern as European capitals.

neighborhoods.body:
Mexico City's neighbourhood variation is sharp, and the reputation of the city as a whole is a poor guide to any part of it.

**Broadly considered safe for daytime tourism:** Roma, Condesa, Polanco, Coyoacán, Centro Histórico and San Ángel. Most visitors will spend their whole trip in these and have no problem.

- **Roma and Condesa** are the standard recommendation for a first visit: walkable, leafy, full of good food, and well connected.
- **Polanco** is upmarket and quiet.
- **Centro Histórico** is spectacular by day and thins out sharply at night.

As anywhere, the useful question is not "is this neighbourhood safe" but "what does the walk from the metro look like at 11pm".
sources: Is Mexico City safe? Honest neighbourhood guide 2026

weather.body:
- **June to September is the rainy season**, with heavy but generally predictable late-afternoon downpours. Plan outdoor activity for the morning.
- **Winter** brings the thermal inversions that produce the worst air-quality days.
- **March to May and October to November** are the most comfortable windows.

The altitude also means the sun is stronger than the temperature suggests, and evenings are cooler than visitors expect year-round — bring a layer.

hidden_costs.body:
Mexico City is genuinely inexpensive by international standards, and there is no significant tourist-tax or resort-fee culture.

The costs that catch people out are small and avoidable: **dynamic currency conversion** at card terminals (always choose pesos), **ATM fees** at standalone machines, and **tipping expectations**, which are real and generally 10–15% in restaurants.

crowds.body:
The pressure points are Teotihuacán mid-morning when the tour buses arrive, the Frida Kahlo Museum — which requires advance booking and regularly sells out — and the Centro Histórico at weekends.

Book the Frida Kahlo Museum well ahead; it is the one thing in the city that reliably catches people out.

entry_requirements.body:
Mexico's entry requirements depend on nationality; many visitors receive a tourist permit on arrival. Check your own government's advice and Mexican official guidance for your dates.

Note that the Quintana Roo departure charge (Visitax) that applies to Cancún and the Riviera Maya does **not** apply to Mexico City — it is a state-level charge.

accommodation.body:
The main practical check is location relative to the Metro and to the neighbourhoods you actually plan to use — Mexico City is very large and a cheap room in the wrong district converts into daily travel time.

Roma and Condesa are the safest default for a first visit: central enough, walkable, and well served.

faqs.q: Will I get altitude sickness in Mexico City?
faqs.a: Possibly, and it is the most common thing to derail a first day. The city sits at 2,240 metres and the drop in available oxygen from sea level is noticeable — headache, fatigue, shortness of breath and disrupted sleep are typical. Most people acclimatise within 24 to 48 hours by staying hydrated, skipping alcohol on the first day and not scheduling anything strenuous. Book the first day light.

faqs.q: How do I get from Mexico City airport without being overcharged?
faqs.a: Use the authorised taxi stands inside the terminal, pre-arranged hotel transport, or Uber/DiDi. Street taxis at the airport frequently refuse the meter, quote inflated prices, or have rigged meters, and touts in the arrivals area quote inflated fares as standard. One 2026 change to know: Uber pickup at the airport is restricted to specific pedestrian-bridge zones — follow the signs for 'App Ride Pickup' rather than waiting at the kerb.

faqs.q: Which Mexico City neighbourhoods are safe for tourists?
faqs.a: Roma, Condesa, Polanco, Coyoacán, Centro Histórico and San Ángel are broadly considered safe for daytime tourism, and most visitors spend their entire trip in them without incident. Petty theft dominates the crime affecting tourists, concentrated on the Metro — particularly the lines serving the airport and popular destinations.

faqs.q: Is the air quality a problem in Mexico City?
faqs.a: It can be. The metropolitan area frequently exceeds WHO pollution guidelines, and it is worst during thermal inversions that trap pollutants over the valley, mostly in winter. On high-pollution days anyone with a respiratory condition should limit outdoor exertion and consider an N95 mask, which is available at any farmacia.

destinations.risk_summary:
Athens has one dominant, entirely solvable problem: **the Acropolis is capped at 20,000 visitors a day** with hourly slot quotas and timed entry, and only **3,000 people** are admitted in the 08:00–09:00 hour. Turning up without a booked slot in season is how people miss the thing they came for.

Tickets are **€30**. Cruise groups arrive between roughly 10:00 and 14:00, which is also when the rock is at its hottest and most exposed.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes. Athens is straightforward, affordable by western European standards and safe in the ordinary big-city sense.

The entire difference between a good Athens trip and a frustrating one is booking the Acropolis slot in advance and taking the earliest one you can get.
destinations.worst_months: July–August (extreme heat plus peak cruise season)

overview.body:
Athens is an easy city to visit with one hard constraint: the Acropolis operates a daily cap and timed entry, and the rest of the trip tends to arrange itself around which slot you got.

Everything else — cost, safety, transport — is unremarkable in the best sense.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes. Athens rewards two or three days properly planned far more than a rushed one, and the museums are genuinely first rank.

If you are travelling in July or August, understand that the Acropolis is an exposed rock with almost no shade and that midday heat there is a real physical problem, not an inconvenience.

top_risks.body:
- **The Acropolis daily cap** of 20,000 with hourly quotas — arrive without a slot in season and you may not get in.
- **Midday heat on the Acropolis**, which has almost no shade.
- **Cruise-group timing**, roughly 10:00–14:00.
- **Taxi overcharging** from the airport and around Syntagma.
- **Pickpocketing** on the metro line to Piraeus and around Monastiraki.
- **Strike days**, which are announced in advance and can close sites and transport.

crowds.body:
**Since September 2023 the Acropolis has limited daily visitors to 20,000, with staggered entry times and hourly slot quotas.** The first hour, 08:00–09:00, admits a maximum of **3,000 people**, with varying limits through the rest of the day.

Book in advance through the official ticketing system. In season, walking up without a slot is not a plan.

**Cruise groups arrive roughly 10:00–14:00**, which compounds both the crowding and the heat. The earliest slot you can get is worth more here than at almost any other European site.
sources: Acropolis introduces cap on daily visitor numbers and staggered entry — Euronews

hidden_costs.body:
- **Acropolis entry: €30.** A combined ticket covering several archaeological sites is available and is better value if you plan to visit more than two.
- **Greek accommodation tax** is charged per room per night, varies by category and season, and is collected at the property rather than at booking.
- **Taxi fares** from the airport to the centre are subject to a published fixed rate; drivers quoting well above it are not offering a service.

Athens is otherwise among the cheaper western European capitals for food and transport.
sources: Acropolis Athens 2026: official tickets and prices

weather.body:
**July and August are genuinely dangerous on the Acropolis.** It is an exposed limestone rock with almost no shade, and Greek authorities have closed it during the hottest hours of severe heatwaves in recent summers.

If you are visiting in high summer, take the earliest slot available, carry water, and treat an afternoon visit as a bad idea rather than a compromise.

April–May and late September–October give you workable temperatures and materially smaller crowds.

scams.body:
- **Taxi overcharging** from the airport and around Syntagma — agree the published fixed airport rate or insist on the meter.
- **The bar/'friendly local' setup**, most reported around Syntagma and Psyrri: a friendly stranger suggests a bar, the bill is enormous and payment is pressured. Do not follow strangers to venues.
- **Unofficial ticket sellers** near the Acropolis entrance, which is a particular problem given the timed-slot system — a resold slot may not be valid.
- **Pickpocketing** on the metro to Piraeus and around Monastiraki and Omonia.

transportation.body:
The metro is clean, cheap and connects the airport, the port at Piraeus and the centre directly.

- **The airport metro line is the simplest arrival** and avoids the taxi negotiation entirely.
- **The Piraeus line** is where pickpocketing concentrates, particularly with luggage on ferry days.
- **Taxis** should use the meter or the published fixed airport rate.
- **Strikes** happen and are announced in advance; they can affect the metro, ferries and archaeological sites.

neighborhoods.body:
- **Plaka and Monastiraki** are the classic visitor bases: central, atmospheric, walkable to the Acropolis, and touristy in pricing.
- **Koukaki** sits just south of the Acropolis and is quieter, cheaper and increasingly the better recommendation.
- **Around Omonia** is the cheapest central accommodation and the least pleasant at night.
- **Exarchia** is characterful and politically active; it is fine but is not a first-visit default.

Check the hill: Athens is steeper than it looks, and "5 minutes from the Acropolis" can mean 5 minutes uphill in 38°C.

entry_requirements.body:
Greece is in the Schengen area. Requirements depend on your nationality and change; check your own government's advice and Greek consular guidance for your dates.

As elsewhere in Europe, passport validity rules catch out more travellers than visa rules.

accommodation.body:
Confirm whether the **accommodation tax** is included — it is charged per room per night, varies by category and season, and is usually collected at the property.

If a rooftop Acropolis view matters to you, confirm it with a photograph from the actual room rather than the listing's hero image; "Acropolis view" is used loosely.

faqs.q: Do I need to book Acropolis tickets in advance?
faqs.a: In season, yes. Since September 2023 the Acropolis has capped daily visitors at 20,000 with staggered entry times and hourly slot quotas — the 08:00–09:00 hour admits a maximum of 3,000 people, with varying limits after that. Entry is €30. Turning up without a booked slot in summer is how people miss the site entirely.

faqs.q: What is the best time of day to visit the Acropolis?
faqs.a: The earliest slot you can get. Cruise groups arrive roughly 10:00 to 14:00, which is also when the site is hottest — it is an exposed limestone rock with almost no shade, and Greek authorities have closed it during the hottest hours of severe heatwaves. Early morning solves the crowd problem and the heat problem at once.

faqs.q: Is Athens expensive?
faqs.a: It is among the cheaper western European capitals for food and transport. The notable costs are Acropolis entry at €30 — a combined archaeological-sites ticket is better value if you will visit more than two — and the Greek accommodation tax, which is charged per room per night, varies by category and season, and is collected at the property rather than at booking.

destinations.risk_summary:
Lisbon's practical risks are **cost creep and crowding**, not danger. The city tax **doubled from €2 to €4 per person per night in September 2024** and has held at €4 through 2026, capped at seven nights; cruise passengers pay a separate **€2 per disembarkation**.

The more common trip-spoiler is physical: Lisbon is built on very steep hills, and a great many visitors underestimate what that means for a walking itinerary and for luggage.
destinations.worth_visiting:
Yes. Lisbon is one of the best-value western European capitals and remains genuinely pleasant outside the peak summer months.

The two things worth planning: the hills (check what your accommodation's address actually involves) and Tram 28, which is a functioning public tram that has become a pickpocketing venue by virtue of being on every itinerary.
destinations.worst_months: July–August (heat and peak crowds)

overview.body:
Lisbon is safe, affordable and easy, and the things that go wrong are mundane: a €4 nightly tax nobody mentioned, a hill nobody warned about, and a tram that is on every list and is therefore where the pickpockets are.

The city has grown considerably as a destination in the last decade and the pressure shows in the historic centre in summer.

worth_visiting.body:
Yes. Lisbon delivers well above its price point, and the day trips — Sintra in particular — are excellent.

Sintra is also the one place that genuinely requires planning: it is extremely busy, several palaces need timed tickets, and it is a full day rather than an afternoon.

top_risks.body:
- **The city tax**, €4 per person per night, capped at 7 nights, collected at the property.
- **The hills.** Lisbon is genuinely steep and this affects itineraries, luggage and accessibility.
- **Pickpocketing on Tram 28** and in Baixa, concentrated because everyone is in the same places.
- **Sintra crowding**, which needs timed tickets and a full day.
- **Summer heat** on stone streets with little shade.
- **Taxi and tuk-tuk overcharging** in the tourist core.

hidden_costs.body:
- **Lisbon city tax: €4 per person per night**, doubled from €2 in September 2024 and held at €4 through 2026. It is **capped at 7 nights** and collected at the property rather than at booking.
- **Cruise passengers** pay a separate **€2 per disembarkation** charge on landing at the Port of Lisbon and entering the city for the day.
- **Tram and funicular single fares bought onboard** are several times the price of the same journey on a rechargeable Viva Viagem card. Get the card at any metro station.
- **Sintra palace tickets** are separate per palace and add up quickly.

Portugal applies tourist taxes regionally, so the Lisbon rate does not apply in Porto or the Algarve.

scams.body:
- **Pickpocketing on Tram 28.** This is a genuine public tram that appears on every visitor itinerary, which is exactly why it is worked. Standing room at the doors is where it happens. The same applies to Tram 15 and crowded lifts.
- **Drug offers in Baixa and Cais do Sodré.** Persistent, low-level, and the substances offered are generally fake. Keep walking.
- **Tuk-tuk pricing** in the tourist core, which is negotiable and frequently starts high.
- **Restaurant couvert.** Bread, olives and cheese placed on the table are chargeable. Sending them back is normal and expected if you do not want them — this is the single most common Portuguese billing surprise.

transportation.body:
- **Get a Viva Viagem card** at any metro station. Fares onboard trams and funiculars are several times the card fare.
- **Tram 28** is the famous one and is a working tram, not a tourist attraction — it is crowded, slow and pickpocketed. Ride it early morning or accept the conditions.
- **The funiculars and the Santa Justa lift** are public transport and covered by the card.
- **Metro from the airport** is direct and cheap.
- **Taxis and tuk-tuks** should be metered or agreed in advance.

crowds.body:
Lisbon's crowding is concentrated in the Baixa–Alfama–Belém corridor and, above all, in **Sintra**.

Sintra needs a full day, timed tickets for the individual palaces, and an early start — the queues for Pena Palace in summer are the single most complained-about experience in the region. Going first thing, or in shoulder season, changes the day completely.

Belém's pastry queue is real but moves fast; the monastery queue does not.

weather.body:
- **July and August** are hot, and Lisbon's hills and stone streets amplify it. There is little shade on the classic walking routes.
- **April to June and September to October** are close to ideal.
- **Winter** is mild but wet, and the polished cobbles (calçada) become genuinely slippery in rain — this causes more visitor injuries than anything criminal.

neighborhoods.body:
**The hills are the real neighbourhood risk in Lisbon**, and listings systematically under-describe them.

- **Alfama** is the most atmospheric and the most vertical. A flat 200 metres from a tram stop can be four flights of steps. With a suitcase this is a serious problem, and taxis frequently cannot reach the door.
- **Bairro Alto** is the nightlife district and is loud until very late, every night in summer.
- **Baixa and Chiado** are flat, central, convenient and priced accordingly.
- **Príncipe Real and Estrela** are quieter, pleasant and a short walk or tram from the centre.

Before booking, look at the address on a street-level map and check both the gradient and whether the building has a lift. Both questions are more consequential here than in most European cities.

entry_requirements.body: Portugal is in the Schengen area. Requirements depend on nationality and change; check your own government's advice and Portuguese consular guidance for your dates, paying particular attention to passport validity rules.

accommodation.body:
Two checks:

1. **Is the €4 per person per night city tax included?** Usually not; it is collected at the property and capped at 7 nights.
2. **Is there a lift, and what is the gradient of the street?** In Alfama and the surrounding hills this is the difference between a good stay and dragging luggage up a staircase — and it is the thing listings are least reliable about.

faqs.q: How much is Lisbon's tourist tax in 2026?
faqs.a: €4 per person per night, capped at 7 nights. It doubled from €2 in September 2024 and has held at €4 through 2026. It is collected at the property rather than at booking. Cruise passengers pay a separate €2 per disembarkation on landing at the Port of Lisbon and entering the city for the day.

faqs.q: Is Tram 28 worth riding?
faqs.a: It is a genuine working public tram on a scenic route, and it is also on every visitor itinerary — which is precisely why it is the most pickpocketed place in Lisbon, particularly in the standing space by the doors. Ride it early in the morning, keep valuables in front pockets, and use a Viva Viagem card rather than paying onboard, which costs several times more.

faqs.q: How steep is Lisbon really?
faqs.a: Steep enough to change how you plan. Alfama in particular is genuinely vertical — a listing 200 flat metres from a tram stop can be four flights of steps up, and taxis often cannot reach the door. The polished cobbles also become slippery in rain. Check the gradient on a street-level map and confirm whether the building has a lift before booking.
